learning_objectives.label: Basic definitions: circle, center, radius, chord, diameter
learning_objectives.description: Define the circle as the set of points of a plane at a constant distance (radius length) from a fixed point (center); classify points as inside, on, or outside the circle; define the surface of the circle, radius, chord, and diameter; congruent circles have equal radii.

questions.stem: The circle is the set of points of a plane which are at a constant distance from a fixed point in the same plane. The fixed point is called … and the constant distance is called …
solution: By the definition of the circle, the fixed point is called the center of the circle.
The constant distance from the center to every point of the circle is called the radius length.
That is why we denote the circle by its center and say: circle M.

questions.stem: A line segment whose end points are any two points on the circle is called …
solution: The chord is a line segment whose end points are any two points on the circle.
A radius has only ONE endpoint on the circle (the other endpoint is the center), so it is not a chord.
A special chord that passes through the center is called a diameter.

questions.stem: For circle M with center M, which of the following statements is correct?
solution: The circle is only the set of points at distance r from the center; the center itself is at distance 0 from itself, so $M \notin$ circle M.
The surface of the circle is the set of points of the circle $\cup$ the set of points inside the circle.
M is a point inside the circle, so $M \in$ surface of circle M.

questions.stem: If the radius length of circle M equals $7$ cm, find the diameter length in cm.
solution: The diameter is the chord passing through the center of the circle, so it is made of two radii.
Diameter length $= 2r = 2 \times 7$.
Diameter length $= 14$ cm.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
solution: The diameter is defined as the chord passing through the center of the circle — so every diameter is a chord, and B is correct.
A is wrong: a chord that does not pass through the center is not a diameter.
C is wrong: a radius has one endpoint at the center, not two endpoints on the circle.
D is wrong: two circles are congruent if their radii are equal in length — concentric circles can have different radii.

learning_objectives.label: The diameter as the longest chord; triangle-inequality arguments
learning_objectives.description: Prove and apply that the diameter is the longest chord in a circle (diameter = 2r); use the triangle inequality with radii (e.g. MN + MD > ND with MD = MB) to compare lengths in circle figures.

questions.stem: The longest chord in a circle is …
solution: The diameter of a circle is its largest chord in length.
Reason: for any chord AB not through the center, the triangle inequality in $\triangle AMB$ gives $AM + MB > AB$, and $AM + MB = 2r$ = diameter length.
So every other chord is shorter than the diameter.

questions.stem: The radius length of circle M is $6.5$ cm. Find the length in cm of the longest chord that can be drawn in circle M.
solution: The longest chord in a circle is the diameter.
Diameter length $= 2r = 2 \times 6.5 = 13$ cm.

questions.stem: In circle M of radius length $r$, $\overline{AB}$ is a chord that does NOT pass through the center. Then $AB \; \square \; 2r$, where $\square$ is …
solution: Join $\overline{MA}$ and $\overline{MB}$; since the chord does not pass through M, the points A, M, B form a triangle.
By the triangle inequality in $\triangle AMB$: $AM + MB > AB$.
$AM = MB = r$ (radii), so $2r > AB$, i.e. $AB < 2r$.

questions.stem: In circle M, $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter, D is a point on the circle, and N is a point on $\overrightarrow{BA}$ outside the circle. Drawing the radius $\overline{MD}$, which result follows?
solution: In $\triangle NMD$, the triangle inequality gives $MN + MD > ND$.
$MD = MB$ because both are radii of circle M.
Substituting: $MN + MB > ND$, and since M lies between N's side and B on the diameter line, $MN + MB = NB$.
Therefore $NB > ND$.

learning_objectives.label: Symmetry in the circle and the chord–center corollaries
learning_objectives.description: Any straight line through the center is an axis of symmetry (infinitely many). Corollaries: (1) the line through the center and the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it; (2) the line through the center perpendicular to a chord bisects it; (3) the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the center. Apply with the Pythagorean theorem to chords and parallel chords.

questions.stem: The number of axes of symmetry of a circle is …
solution: Any straight line passing through the center of a circle is an axis of symmetry of it.
There is an infinite number of straight lines passing through the center.
So the circle has an infinite number of axes of symmetry.

questions.stem: In circle M, $\overline{MC} \perp \overline{AB}$ where $\overline{AB}$ is a chord and $C \in \overline{AB}$. Then C is …
solution: Corollary: the straight line passing through the center of a circle and perpendicular to any chord of it bisects this chord.
$\overline{MC}$ passes through the center M and is perpendicular to the chord $\overline{AB}$.
So C is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$, i.e. $AC = CB$.

questions.stem: In circle M of radius length $13$ cm, $\overline{AB}$ is a chord of length $24$ cm. Find the distance in cm of the chord from the center M.
solution: Let X be the point where the perpendicular from M meets $\overline{AB}$; the line through the center perpendicular to a chord bisects it, so $AX = \dfrac{24}{2} = 12$ cm.
In the right-angled triangle $AXM$: $(MX)^2 + (AX)^2 = (AM)^2$.
$MX = 5$ cm.

questions.stem: In circle M of radius length $10$ cm, a chord $\overline{CD}$ is at distance $6$ cm from the center. Find the length of $\overline{CD}$ in cm.
solution: Let X be the foot of the perpendicular from M on $\overline{CD}$; then X is the midpoint of the chord (corollary).
In the right-angled triangle $MXC$: $(CX)^2 = r^2 - (MX)^2 = 10^2 - 6^2 = 100 - 36 = 64$, so $CX = 8$ cm.
$CD = 2 \times CX = 16$ cm.

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ are two parallel chords in circle M lying on OPPOSITE sides of the center, $AB = 10$ cm, $CD = 24$ cm, and the radius length is $13$ cm. Find the distance in cm between the two chords.
solution: The perpendicular from M to two parallel chords lies on one straight line, meeting $\overline{AB}$ at its midpoint X and $\overline{CD}$ at its midpoint Y.
Distance of $\overline{AB}$: $(MX)^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144$, so $MX = 12$ cm.
Distance of $\overline{CD}$: $(MY)^2 = 13^2 - 12^2 = 169 - 144 = 25$, so $MY = 5$ cm.
The chords are on opposite sides of the center, so the distance between them $= MX + MY = 12 + 5 = 17$ cm.
(If they were on the same side, the distance would be $12 - 5 = 7$ cm — that is why the drill asks whether there are other answers.)

learning_objectives.label: Position of a point with respect to a circle
learning_objectives.description: For circle M with radius length r and point A in its plane: A is outside the circle iff MA > r, on the circle iff MA = r, inside iff MA < r (and vice versa); solve equations and inequalities on MA.

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $4$ cm and A is a point in its plane where $MA = 4$ cm. Then A is …
solution: A point A is on circle M if and only if $MA = r$.
Here $MA = 4$ cm $= r$, so A is on the circle.

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $4$ cm and $MA = 2\sqrt{3}$ cm. Then A is …
solution: Compare $MA$ with the radius length: $MA = 2\sqrt{3} = \sqrt{12}$ and $r = 4 = \sqrt{16}$.
$\sqrt{12} < \sqrt{16}$, so $MA < r$.
$MA < r$ means A is located inside the circle.

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $4$ cm and $MA = 3\sqrt{2}$ cm. Then A is …
solution: $MA = 3\sqrt{2} = \sqrt{18}$ and $r = 4 = \sqrt{16}$.
$\sqrt{18} > \sqrt{16}$, so $MA > r$.
$MA > r$ means A is located outside the circle.

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $4$ cm and $MA =$ zero. Then …
solution: $MA = 0$ means the distance between A and M is zero, so the point A is the center M itself.
Since $MA = 0 < r = 4$, the point A (the center) is inside the circle.

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $5$ cm, A is a point in its plane and $MA = (2x - 3)$ cm. If A is located OUTSIDE the circle, then …
solution: Point A is located outside circle M, so $MA > r$, i.e. $MA > 5$.

learning_objectives.label: Position of a straight line with respect to a circle; tangents
learning_objectives.description: With MA ⊥ L at A: the line is outside the circle iff MA > r, a secant (two common points) iff MA < r, a tangent (one common point) iff MA = r. A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency; a line perpendicular to a diameter at an endpoint is a tangent.

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $7$ cm, L is a straight line in its plane and $\overline{MA} \perp L$ at $A \in L$ with $MA = 7$ cm. Then L is …
solution: Compare the distance MA with the radius length: $MA = 7 = r$.
When $MA = r$, the straight line L is tangent to circle M, and it has exactly one common point with the circle: $L \cap$ the circle $= \{A\}$.

questions.stem: Circle M has radius length $7$ cm and the distance between its center and the straight line L is $MA = 4\sqrt{3}$ cm. Then L …
solution: $MA = 4\sqrt{3} = \sqrt{48}$ and $r = 7 = \sqrt{49}$.
$\sqrt{48} < \sqrt{49}$, so $MA < r$.
When $MA < r$, the straight line L is a secant to the circle: $L \cap$ circle M $= \{C, D\}$, two points.

questions.stem: L is a tangent to circle M at the point A. Then the measure of the angle between L and the radius $\overline{MA}$ equals …
solution: Important fact: a tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at its point of tangency.
So $L \perp \overline{MA}$, and the measure of the angle between them is $90°$.

questions.stem: $\overline{XY}$ is a tangent to circle M at X, the radius length is $5$ cm, and $MY = 13$ cm. Find the length of $\overline{XY}$ in cm.
solution: The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency, so $\overline{MX} \perp \overline{XY}$ and $\triangle MXY$ is right-angled at X.
By the Pythagorean theorem: $(XY)^2 = (MY)^2 - (MX)^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144$.
$XY = 12$ cm.

questions.stem: The straight line L intersects circle M of radius length $7$ cm in two points, and the distance from the center to L is $MA = (3x - 5)$ cm. Then …
solution: L intersects the circle in two points (a secant), so $MA < r$: $3x - 5 < 7$, giving $3x < 12$, i.e. $x < 4$.
MA is a distance, so $MA \geq 0$: $3x - 5 \geq 0$, giving $x \geq \dfrac{5}{3}$.
Together: $\dfrac{5}{3} \leq x < 4$.

learning_objectives.label: Position of a circle with respect to another circle
learning_objectives.description: For circles M, N with radii r1 > r2: distant iff MN > r1 + r2; touching externally iff MN = r1 + r2; intersecting iff r1 − r2 < MN < r1 + r2; touching internally iff MN = r1 − r2; one inside the other iff MN < r1 − r2 (concentric when MN = 0). The line of centers of touching circles passes through the point of tangency perpendicular to the common tangent; the line of centers of intersecting circles is perpendicular to the common chord and bisects it.

questions.stem: Circles M and N have radii lengths $9$ cm and $4$ cm respectively, and $MN = 13$ cm. Then the two circles are …
solution: When $MN = r_1 + r_2$, the two circles are touching externally (one common point between the two centers).

questions.stem: Circles M and N have radii lengths $9$ cm and $4$ cm respectively, and $MN = 5$ cm. Then the two circles are …
solution: When $MN = r_1 - r_2$, the two circles are touching internally (one common point, the smaller circle inside the larger).

questions.stem: Circles M and N have radii lengths $8$ cm and $3$ cm respectively, and $MN = 6$ cm. Then the two circles are …
solution: In this case the two circles are intersecting: they have two common points and a common chord.

questions.stem: Two circles M and N of radii lengths $8$ cm and $5$ cm are touching externally. Find the distance $MN$ between their centers in cm.
solution: Two circles are touching externally when the distance between their centers equals the sum of their radii.

questions.stem: M and N are two circles intersecting at A and B, $AM = 9$ cm, $AN = 12$ cm and $\overline{MA} \perp \overline{AN}$. Find the length of the common chord $\overline{AB}$ in cm.
solution: $\triangle MAN$ is right-angled at A, so $MN = \sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{81 + 144} = \sqrt{225} = 15$ cm.
The line of centers of two intersecting circles is perpendicular to the common chord and bisects it; let it cut $\overline{AB}$ at C.
$\overline{AC}$ is the height to the hypotenuse of the right triangle: $AC \times MN = AM \times AN$, so $AC = \dfrac{9 \times 12}{15} = 7.2$ cm.
$AB = 2 \times AC = 14.4$ cm.

learning_objectives.label: Identifying the circle through given points; the circumcircle
learning_objectives.description: Infinitely many circles pass through one point, or through two points (centers on the axis of the segment; smallest radius = half the segment). One and only one circle passes through three noncollinear points; none through collinear points. The circumcircle of a triangle has its center at the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides.

questions.stem: The number of circles which pass through three noncollinear points is …
solution: There is one and only one circle which passes through three noncollinear points.
Its center is the intersection point of the axes (perpendicular bisectors) of the two segments joining the points, and this intersection is a single point.

questions.stem: A and B are two given points. The centers of all the circles passing through both A and B are located on …
solution: If a circle passes through A and B, then $\overline{AB}$ is a chord in it.
The perpendicular bisector of any chord of a circle passes through the center of the circle.
So every such center lies on the axis of $\overline{AB}$ — and every point of the axis can serve as a center, giving an infinite number of circles.

questions.stem: A and B are two points where $AB = 8$ cm. Find in cm the radius length of the smallest circle that can be drawn passing through A and B.
solution: The radius length of the smallest circle that can be drawn to pass through the two points A and B equals $\dfrac{1}{2} AB$.
That smallest circle is the one taking $\overline{AB}$ itself as a diameter, centered at the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$.
Radius $= \dfrac{8}{2} = 4$ cm.

questions.stem: A, B and C are three collinear points. How many circles pass through the three points A, B and C together?
solution: The center of such a circle would have to lie on the axis $L_1$ of $\overline{AB}$ and on the axis $L_2$ of $\overline{BC}$.
When A, B, C are collinear, $L_1 \parallel L_2$, so $L_1 \cap L_2 = \phi$ — there is no possible center.
So no circle can be drawn passing through three collinear points.

questions.stem: To locate the center of the circumcircle of triangle ABC (the circle passing through its vertices), we draw …
solution: The circle which passes through the vertices of a triangle is called the circumcircle of this triangle, and the triangle is said to be inscribed in the circle.
Corollary: the perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle intersect at a point which is the center of the circumcircle.
Each vertex-pair (side) is a chord of the circumcircle, and the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the center — so their common point is the center.

learning_objectives.label: Chord length versus distance from the center
learning_objectives.description: Using (MX)² + (AX)² = r² for a chord with midpoint X: the closer the chord is to the center of the circle, the longer it is, and vice versa; compare chords and solve for unknown lengths.

questions.stem: In circle M, chord $\overline{AB}$ is at distance $3$ cm from the center and chord $\overline{CD}$ is at distance $5$ cm from the center. Then $AB \; \square \; CD$, where $\square$ is …
solution: Rule: the closer the chord is to the center of the circle, the longer its length is, and vice versa.
$\overline{AB}$ is at distance 3 cm, which is closer to the center than $\overline{CD}$ at 5 cm.
So $AB > CD$.

questions.stem: In circle M, $AB = 8$ cm and $CD = 6$ cm are two chords, $\overline{MX} \perp \overline{AB}$ and $\overline{MY} \perp \overline{CD}$. Then $MX \; \square \; MY$, where $\square$ is …
solution: The longer chord is the closer one to the center (the rule 'closer ⟺ longer' read in reverse).
$AB = 8 > CD = 6$, so $\overline{AB}$ is closer to the center than $\overline{CD}$.
MX is the distance of $\overline{AB}$ and MY is the distance of $\overline{CD}$, so $MX < MY$.

questions.stem: In circle M of radius length $13$ cm, chord $\overline{AB}$ is at distance $5$ cm from the center and chord $\overline{CD}$ is at distance $12$ cm. Find $AB - CD$ in cm.
solution: For a chord at distance d from the center, half the chord $= \sqrt{r^2 - d^2}$ (from $(MX)^2 + (AX)^2 = r^2$).
$AB - CD = 24 - 10 = 14$ cm — the closer chord (5 cm away) is indeed the longer one.

questions.stem: In circle M, chord $\overline{CD} = (x + 2)$ cm is at distance $4$ cm from the center, and chord $\overline{AB} = 8$ cm is at distance $6$ cm from the center. Then …
solution: $\overline{CD}$ is at distance 4 cm and $\overline{AB}$ at 6 cm, so $\overline{CD}$ is closer to the center.
The closer the chord is to the center, the longer it is: $CD > AB$.

learning_objectives.label: Equal chords are equidistant from the center, and the converse
learning_objectives.description: Theorem: chords of a circle equal in length are equidistant from the center (also in congruent circles). Converse: in the same circle or congruent circles, chords equidistant from the center(s) are equal in length. Applications to inscribed isosceles triangles.

questions.stem: In circle M, $AB = CD$ are two chords, $\overline{MX} \perp \overline{AB}$ and $\overline{MY} \perp \overline{CD}$. Then …
solution: Theorem: if chords of a circle are equal in length, then they are equidistant from the center.
MX and MY are the distances of the two chords from the center.
$AB = CD$, so $MX = MY$.

questions.stem: In circle M, $\overline{MX} \perp \overline{AB}$, $\overline{MY} \perp \overline{CD}$, $MX = MY$ and $YD = 7$ cm. Find the length of $\overline{AB}$ in cm.
solution: $\overline{MY}$ passes through the center perpendicular to the chord $\overline{CD}$, so it bisects it: $CD = 2 \times YD = 14$ cm.
Converse of the theorem: in the same circle, chords which are equidistant from the center are equal in length.
$MX = MY$, so $AB = CD = 14$ cm.

questions.stem: In circle M, the chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ are equal in length. The distance of $\overline{AB}$ from the center is $(2x + 1)$ cm and the distance of $\overline{CD}$ from the center is $9$ cm. Find the value of $x$.
solution: If chords of a circle are equal in length, then they are equidistant from the center.

questions.stem: Triangle ABC is inscribed in circle M with $m(\angle B) = m(\angle C)$. X is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{MY} \perp \overline{AC}$. Which chain of reasoning proves $MX = MY$?
solution: In $\triangle ABC$: $m(\angle B) = m(\angle C)$, so the sides opposite to them are equal: $AC = AB$ (isosceles triangle).

$\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ are two chords of circle M, and X is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$, so $\overline{MX} \perp \overline{AB}$ (line through the center and a chord's midpoint is perpendicular to it) — MX and MY are the two chords' distances from the center.
If chords of a circle are equal in length, then they are equidistant from the center: $AB = AC \Rightarrow MX = MY$.

questions.stem: Triangle ABC is inscribed in circle M, $\overline{MD} \perp \overline{AB}$, $\overline{ME} \perp \overline{AC}$, $MD = ME$ and $m(\angle B) = 70°$. Find $m(\angle A)$ in degrees.
solution: $MD$ and $ME$ are the distances of the chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ from the center, and $MD = ME$.
Converse of the theorem: chords which are equidistant from the center are equal in length, so $AB = AC$.
$\triangle ABC$ is isosceles, so $m(\angle C) = m(\angle B) = 70°$.

learning_objectives.label: Central angle and the measure of arcs
learning_objectives.description: Define the central angle (its vertex is the center of the circle and its two sides are radii); the two sides divide the circle into a minor arc AB and a major arc ACB; measure of the arc = measure of the central angle opposite to it; measure of the semicircle = 180° and of the whole circle = 360°; adjacent arcs share exactly one point and their measures add: m(AB) + m(BC) = m(ABC).

questions.stem: The central angle is the angle whose vertex is … and whose two sides are …
solution: By definition, the central angle is the angle whose vertex is the center of the circle and the two sides are radii in the circle.
An angle whose vertex lies ON the circle with sides containing two chords is a different angle — the inscribed angle (lesson 5-2).

questions.stem: The measure of the semicircle equals … and the measure of the whole circle equals …
solution: The measure of the arc is the measure of the central angle opposite to it.
If $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter, $\angle AMB$ is a straight angle of measure $180°$, so the measure of the semicircle $= 180°$.
The two semicircles make the whole circle: measure of a circle $= 180° + 180° = 360°$.

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter in circle M, $\overline{MC} \perp \overline{AB}$, and D is a point on the circle between A and C where $m(\angle AMD) = 50°$. Find $m(\overset{\frown}{DC})$ in degrees.
solution: $\overline{MC} \perp \overline{AB}$, so $m(\angle AMC) = 90°$, and the measure of the arc is the measure of the central angle opposite to it: $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = 90°$.
D lies between A and C, so $m(\angle DMC) = m(\angle AMC) - m(\angle AMD) = 90° - 50° = 40°$.
$m(\overset{\frown}{DC}) = m(\angle DMC) = 40°$.

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter in circle M, the points C and D lie on the same side of it (in the order A, C, D, B), $m(\angle CMD) = 60°$ and $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) : m(\overset{\frown}{DB}) = 3 : 5$. Find $m(\overset{\frown}{ACD})$ in degrees.
solution: Suppose that $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = 3x°$, so $m(\overset{\frown}{DB}) = 5x°$.
$\overline{AB}$ is a diameter, so the arcs on one side add to a semicircle: $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) + m(\overset{\frown}{CD}) + m(\overset{\frown}{DB}) = 180°$.
$3x + 60 + 5x = 180$, so $8x = 120$ and $x = 15$: $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = 45°$, $m(\overset{\frown}{DB}) = 75°$.
Adjacent arcs add: $m(\overset{\frown}{ACD}) = m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) + m(\overset{\frown}{CD}) = 45° + 60° = 105°$.

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter in circle M and the points C, D lie on the same side of it in the order A, C, D, B, where $m(\angle AMC) = 2x°$, $m(\angle CMD) = 3x°$ and $m(\angle DMB) = 4x°$. Find $m(\overset{\frown}{CD})$ in degrees.
solution: The three central angles together make the straight angle $\angle AMB$: $2x + 3x + 4x = 180$.
The measure of the arc is the measure of the central angle opposite to it: $m(\overset{\frown}{CD}) = m(\angle CMD) = 3x° = 60°$.

learning_objectives.label: Arc length as a part of the circumference
learning_objectives.description: Arc length is a part of a circle's circumference proportional with its measure: arc length = (measure of the arc / measure of the circle) × circumference. Compute arc lengths; in concentric circles the same central angle gives arcs equal in measure but different in length, so equal measures give equal lengths only in the same circle or congruent circles (Corollary 1).

questions.stem: The arc length equals …
solution: Arc length is a part of a circle's circumference proportional with its measure.
Arc length $= \dfrac{\text{the measure of the arc}}{\text{the measure of the circle}} \times$ circumference of the circle, where the measure of the circle is $360°$.
Note the difference: the measure of an arc is in degrees; the length of an arc is in length units (cm).

questions.stem: M is a circle with radius length $7$ cm and $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 90°$. Find the length of $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ in cm. $\left(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\right)$
solution: Arc length $= \dfrac{\text{measure of the arc}}{\text{measure of the circle}} \times$ circumference of the circle.
Circumference $= 2\pi r = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 = 44$ cm.
Length of $\overset{\frown}{AB} = \dfrac{90}{360} \times 44 = \dfrac{44}{4} = 11$ cm.

questions.stem: M is a circle with radius length $10$ cm and $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 72°$. Find the length of $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ in cm. $(\pi = 3.14)$
solution: Circumference of the circle $= 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 10 = 62.8$ cm.
Arc length $= \dfrac{\text{measure of the arc}}{\text{measure of the circle}} \times$ circumference $= \dfrac{72}{360} \times 62.8$.
$\dfrac{72}{360} = \dfrac{1}{5}$, so the length of $\overset{\frown}{AB} = \dfrac{62.8}{5} = 12.56$ cm.

questions.stem: Two concentric circles at M have radii lengths $7$ cm and $14$ cm. The same central angle of measure $90°$ cuts arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ from the minor circle and arc $\overset{\frown}{CD}$ from the major circle. $\left(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\right)$ Which statement is correct?
solution: Both arcs are opposite to the same central angle, so $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{CD}) = 90°$.
Length of $\overset{\frown}{AB} = \dfrac{90}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 = \dfrac{44}{4} = 11$ cm.
Length of $\overset{\frown}{CD} = \dfrac{90}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 = \dfrac{88}{4} = 22$ cm $= 2 \times 11$ cm.
Corollary 1 (equal measures ⟹ equal lengths) holds only in the same circle or in congruent circles — concentric circles of different radii are not congruent, so the arcs are not congruent.

questions.stem: In circle M of radius length $10$ cm, the length of $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ is $15.7$ cm. Find $m(\overset{\frown}{AB})$ in degrees. $(\pi = 3.14)$
solution: Circumference $= 2\pi r = 2 \times 3.14 \times 10 = 62.8$ cm.
Arc length $= \dfrac{\text{measure of the arc}}{360} \times$ circumference, so $15.7 = \dfrac{m(\overset{\frown}{AB})}{360} \times 62.8$.
$m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = \dfrac{15.7}{62.8} \times 360 = \dfrac{1}{4} \times 360 = 90°$.

learning_objectives.label: Arc–chord corollaries: equal arcs, equal chords, parallel chords and tangents
learning_objectives.description: In the same circle or congruent circles: arcs equal in measure have equal lengths and equal chords, and conversely (Corollaries 1–2); two parallel chords cut off equal arcs between them (Corollary 3); a chord parallel to a tangent cuts off equal arcs between them (Corollary 4). Apply with arc addition/subtraction to inscribed quadrilaterals (AC = BD ⟹ AB = DC).

questions.stem: In the same circle M, if $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{CD})$, then …
solution: Corollary 2: in the same circle (or in congruent circles), if the measures of arcs are equal, then their chords are equal in length, and conversely.
$m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{CD})$, so the length of $\overline{AB}$ = the length of $\overline{CD}$.

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ are two chords in circle M where $\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{CD}$. Then …
solution: Corollary 3: if two parallel chords are drawn in a circle, then the measures of the two arcs between them are equal.
$\overline{AB} \parallel \overline{CD}$, so $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = m(\overset{\frown}{BD})$ — the two arcs between the parallel chords.

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ are two parallel chords in circle M, and the arcs between them have measures $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = (2x + 10)°$ and $m(\overset{\frown}{BD}) = 50°$. Find the value of $x$.
solution: If two parallel chords are drawn in a circle, then the measures of the two arcs between them are equal (Corollary 3).

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ is a chord of circle M, and $\overleftrightarrow{CD}$ is a tangent to the circle at C where $\overline{AB} \parallel \overleftrightarrow{CD}$. Then …
solution: Corollary 4: if a chord is parallel to a tangent of a circle, then the measures of the two arcs between them are equal.
$\overline{AB} \parallel \overleftrightarrow{CD}$ (tangent at C), so $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = m(\overset{\frown}{BC})$.
The two equal arcs meet at C, so C bisects the arc $\overset{\frown}{ACB}$.

questions.stem: ABCD is a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle in which $AC = BD$, $AB = (2x - 3)$ cm and $CD = (x + 4)$ cm. Find the length of $\overline{AB}$ in cm.
solution: $AC = BD$ (equal chords), so their arcs are equal in measure: $m(\overset{\frown}{ABC}) = m(\overset{\frown}{BCD})$ (Corollary 2, conversely).

Subtract the common arc $\overset{\frown}{BC}$ from both: $m(\overset{\frown}{ABC}) - m(\overset{\frown}{BC}) = m(\overset{\frown}{BCD}) - m(\overset{\frown}{BC})$, so $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{DC})$.
Equal arcs have equal chords: $AB = CD$, so $2x - 3 = x + 4$.
$x = 7$, so $AB = 2 \times 7 - 3 = 11$ cm.

questions.stem: ABCD is a quadrilateral inscribed in circle M, $\overline{AC}$ is a diameter in the circle and $CB = CD$. Which chain of reasoning proves that $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{AD})$?
solution: $CB = CD$, and equal chords have arcs equal in measure (Corollary 2, conversely): $m(\overset{\frown}{CB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{CD})$.

$\overline{AC}$ is a diameter, so each of $\overset{\frown}{ABC}$ and $\overset{\frown}{ADC}$ is a semicircle of measure $180°$: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 180° - m(\overset{\frown}{CB})$ and $m(\overset{\frown}{AD}) = 180° - m(\overset{\frown}{CD})$.
Subtracting equal measures from $180°$ gives equal results: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{AD})$.

learning_objectives.label: The inscribed angle and its relation to the central angle
learning_objectives.description: Define the inscribed angle (vertex on the circle, sides contain two chords); for each inscribed angle there is one central angle subtended by the same arc, but infinitely many inscribed angles. Theorem: the measure of the inscribed angle is half the measure of the central angle subtended by the same arc; apply it, including with the tangent-perpendicular-to-radius fact.

questions.stem: The inscribed angle is an angle …
solution: By definition, the inscribed angle is an angle the vertex of it lies on the circle and its sides contain two chords of the circle.
The angle whose vertex is the center with radii as sides is the central angle — for each inscribed angle there is one central angle subtended by the same arc.

questions.stem: In circle M, $\angle ACB$ is an inscribed angle and $\angle AMB$ is a central angle, both subtended by $\overset{\frown}{AB}$. If $m(\angle AMB) = 100°$, find $m(\angle ACB)$ in degrees.
solution: Theorem: the measure of the inscribed angle is half the measure of the central angle, subtended by the same arc.
$m(\angle ACB) = \dfrac{1}{2}\, m(\angle AMB) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 100° = 50°$.

questions.stem: In circle M, the inscribed angle $\angle ACB$ and the central angle $\angle AMB$ are subtended by the same arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}$. If $m(\angle ACB) = 35°$, find $m(\angle AMB)$ in degrees.
solution: The measure of the inscribed angle is half the measure of the central angle, subtended by the same arc.
So the central angle is double the inscribed angle: $m(\angle AMB) = 2\, m(\angle ACB)$.
$m(\angle AMB) = 2 \times 35° = 70°$.

questions.stem: In circle M, the central angle $\angle AMB$ of measure $(2x + 20)°$ and an inscribed angle of measure $40°$ are subtended by the same arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}$. Find the value of $x$.
solution: The measure of the inscribed angle is half the measure of the central angle subtended by the same arc, so the central angle $= 2 \times 40° = 80°$.

questions.stem: A is a point outside circle M, $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is a tangent to the circle at B, and $\overrightarrow{AM}$ intersects the circle at C and D respectively, where $m(\angle A) = 50°$. Find $m(\angle BDC)$ in degrees.
solution: $\overrightarrow{AB}$ is a tangent to the circle at B and $\overline{BM}$ is a radius, so $m(\angle ABM) = 90°$ (the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency).
In $\triangle ABM$: $m(\angle BMC) = 180° - (50° + 90°) = 40°$ (C lies on the ray $\overrightarrow{MA}$, so $\angle BMA$ and $\angle BMC$ are the same angle).
The inscribed $\angle BDC$ and the central $\angle BMC$ are both subtended by $\overset{\frown}{BC}$.
The measure of the inscribed angle is half the measure of the central angle subtended by the same arc: $m(\angle BDC) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 40° = 20°$.

questions.stem: In circle M, how many inscribed angles are subtended by the same arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ as the central angle $\angle AMB$?
solution: An inscribed angle subtended by $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ has its vertex at any point of the opposite arc and its sides passing through A and B.
The opposite arc contains an infinite number of points, so there is an infinite number of such inscribed angles.
For each inscribed angle there is only ONE central angle subtended by the same arc — but not the other way around.

learning_objectives.label: Inscribed angle equals half the subtended arc; the angle in a semicircle
learning_objectives.description: Corollary 1: the measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of the subtended arc. Corollary 2: the inscribed angle drawn in a semicircle is a right angle. Classify inscribed angles by comparing the subtended arc with a semicircle (less ⟹ acute, greater ⟹ obtuse); solve arc-ratio problems around the full 360°.

questions.stem: The inscribed angle drawn in a semicircle is …
solution: Corollary 2: the inscribed angle drawn in a semicircle is a right angle.
Reason: the arc opposite to it is a semicircle, $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 180°$, and the inscribed angle is half the subtended arc: $m(\angle C) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 180° = 90°$.

questions.stem: In circle M, the inscribed angle $\angle ACB$ is subtended by $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ where $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 84°$. Find $m(\angle ACB)$ in degrees.
solution: Corollary 1: the measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of the subtended arc.
$m(\angle ACB) = \dfrac{1}{2}\, m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 84° = 42°$.

questions.stem: ABC is an inscribed triangle in circle M where $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) : m(\overset{\frown}{BC}) : m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = 5 : 4 : 3$. Find $m(\angle ACB)$ in degrees.
solution: Suppose that $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 5x°$, $m(\overset{\frown}{BC}) = 4x°$, $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = 3x°$.
The arcs make the whole circle: $5x + 4x + 3x = 360$, so $12x = 360$ and $x = 30$.
$m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 5 \times 30 = 150°$, and it is opposite to the inscribed $\angle ACB$.
The measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of the subtended arc: $m(\angle ACB) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 150° = 75°$.

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter in circle M and C is a point on the circle where $m(\angle CAB) = 35°$. Find $m(\angle CBA)$ in degrees.
solution: $\angle ACB$ is an inscribed angle drawn in a semicircle (its opposite arc is the semicircle on diameter $\overline{AB}$), so $m(\angle ACB) = 90°$ (Corollary 2).
In $\triangle ABC$: $m(\angle CBA) = 180° - (90° + 35°)$.
$m(\angle CBA) = 55°$.

questions.stem: The inscribed angle opposite to an arc LESS than a semicircle is …
solution: The measure of an inscribed angle is half the measure of the subtended arc (Corollary 1).
If the arc is less than a semicircle, its measure $< 180°$, so the inscribed angle $< \dfrac{1}{2} \times 180° = 90°$: the angle is acute.
Similarly, an arc greater than a semicircle gives an obtuse inscribed angle, and exactly a semicircle gives a right angle.

learning_objectives.label: Angles of chords meeting inside or outside the circle
learning_objectives.description: Well-known problem 1: if two chords intersect at a point inside a circle, the measure of the included angle equals half the sum of the measures of the two opposite arcs. Well-known problem 2: if two rays carrying two chords intersect outside the circle, the measure of their angle equals half the difference of the measures of the far and near intercepted arcs.

questions.stem: If two chords intersect at a point inside a circle, then the measure of the included angle equals …
solution: Well-known problem (1): if two chords intersect at a point inside a circle, then the measure of the included angle equals half of the sum of the measure of the two opposite arcs.
For $\overline{AB} \cap \overline{CD} = \{E\}$: $m(\angle AEC) = \dfrac{1}{2}\,[\,m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) + m(\overset{\frown}{BD})\,]$.
The proof draws $\overline{AD}$ and uses the exterior angle of $\triangle AED$ with Corollary 1 on each inscribed angle.

questions.stem: In circle M, the two chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ intersect at E inside the circle, $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = 70°$ and $m(\overset{\frown}{BD}) = 40°$. Find $m(\angle AEC)$ in degrees.
solution: Two chords intersecting inside the circle: the included angle equals half the sum of the two opposite arcs.
$m(\angle AEC) = \dfrac{1}{2}\,[\,m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) + m(\overset{\frown}{BD})\,] = \dfrac{1}{2}\,(70° + 40°)$.
$m(\angle AEC) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 110° = 55°$.

questions.stem: From the point E outside circle M, two rays are drawn carrying two chords: the first cuts the circle at B then A, and the second cuts it at D then C. If $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = 120°$ and $m(\overset{\frown}{BD}) = 40°$, find $m(\angle E)$ in degrees.
solution: Well-known problem (2): when the two rays intersect outside the circle, the measure of their angle equals half the measure of the far (major) arc minus half the measure of the near (minor) arc included between the two sides.
$m(\angle E) = \dfrac{1}{2}\,[\,m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) - m(\overset{\frown}{BD})\,] = \dfrac{1}{2}\,(120° - 40°)$.
$m(\angle E) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 80° = 40°$.

questions.stem: $\overrightarrow{CB} \cap \overrightarrow{ED} = \{A\}$ outside circle M, $m(\angle A) = 35°$ and the inscribed angle $m(\angle BCD) = 25°$. Find $m(\overset{\frown}{CE})$ in degrees.
solution: $\angle BCD$ is an inscribed angle subtended by $\overset{\frown}{BD}$, so $m(\overset{\frown}{BD}) = 2\,m(\angle BCD) = 2 \times 25° = 50°$ (Corollary 1).
The two rays through A intersect outside the circle, so $m(\angle A) = \dfrac{1}{2}\,[\,m(\overset{\frown}{CE}) - m(\overset{\frown}{BD})\,]$.
$35 = \dfrac{1}{2}\,[\,m(\overset{\frown}{CE}) - 50\,]$, so $m(\overset{\frown}{CE}) - 50 = 70$.
$m(\overset{\frown}{CE}) = 120°$.

questions.stem: In circle M, the two chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ intersect at E inside the circle, $m(\angle AEC) = 65°$, $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = (3x + 10)°$ and $m(\overset{\frown}{BD}) = 60°$. Find the value of $x$.
solution: The included angle of two chords intersecting inside the circle equals half the sum of the two opposite arcs: $m(\angle AEC) = \dfrac{1}{2}\,[\,m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) + m(\overset{\frown}{BD})\,]$.
Check: $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = 70°$ and $\dfrac{1}{2}(70 + 60) = 65$ ✓.

learning_objectives.label: Inscribed angles subtended by the same arc are equal (Theorem 2)
learning_objectives.description: Theorem 2: in the same circle, the measures of all inscribed angles subtended by the same arc are equal in measure (each equals half the measure of that arc). Use it in angle chases with intersecting chords and inscribed quadrilaterals (e.g. EA = ED at the intersection of two chords forces EB = EC).

questions.stem: In the same circle, the measures of all inscribed angles subtended by the same arc are …
solution: Theorem 2: in the same circle, the measures of all inscribed angles subtended by the same arc are equal in measure.
Proof idea: each of them equals half the measure of the same subtended arc — $m(\angle C) = m(\angle D) = m(\angle E) = \dfrac{1}{2}\,m(\overset{\frown}{AB})$.

questions.stem: In circle M, $\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$ are two inscribed angles subtended by the same arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}$, and $m(\angle ACB) = 48°$. Find $m(\angle ADB)$ in degrees.
solution: In the same circle, the measures of all inscribed angles subtended by the same arc are equal in measure (Theorem 2).
$m(\angle ADB) = m(\angle ACB) = 48°$.

questions.stem: In circle M, $\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$ are inscribed angles subtended by the same arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}$, where $m(\angle ACB) = (5x - 40)°$ and $m(\angle ADB) = 30°$. Find the value of $x$.
solution: Inscribed angles subtended by the same arc are equal in measure (Theorem 2): $5x - 40 = 30$.

questions.stem: ABCD is a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle whose diagonals $\overline{AC}$ and $\overline{BD}$ intersect at E, $m(\angle DAC) = 30°$ and $m(\angle ADB) = 45°$. Find $m(\angle DEC)$ in degrees.
solution: E lies on $\overline{AC}$ and on $\overline{BD}$, so in $\triangle AED$: $m(\angle EAD) = m(\angle CAD) = 30°$ and $m(\angle ADE) = m(\angle ADB) = 45°$.
$\angle DEC$ is an exterior angle of $\triangle AED$ at E, so $m(\angle DEC) = m(\angle EAD) + m(\angle ADE) = 30° + 45° = 75°$.

Check with the intersecting-chords rule: $\angle DAC$ inscribed on $\overset{\frown}{DC}$ gives $m(\overset{\frown}{DC}) = 60°$; $\angle ADB$ inscribed on $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ gives $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 90°$; then $m(\angle DEC) = \dfrac{1}{2}(60° + 90°) = 75°$ ✓.
(By Theorem 2, $m(\angle DBC) = m(\angle DAC) = 30°$ as well — both are inscribed on $\overset{\frown}{DC}$.)

questions.stem: In a circle, the two chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{CD}$ intersect at E inside the circle where $EA = ED$. Which chain of reasoning proves that $EB = EC$?
solution: In $\triangle AED$: $EA = ED$, so $m(\angle D) = m(\angle A)$ (base angles of an isosceles triangle).

$\angle ABC$ and $\angle ADC$ are both inscribed and include $\overset{\frown}{AC}$, so $m(\angle B) = m(\angle D)$; $\angle DCB$ and $\angle DAB$ are both inscribed and include $\overset{\frown}{BD}$, so $m(\angle C) = m(\angle A)$ (Theorem 2).
Therefore $m(\angle B) = m(\angle C)$, and in $\triangle EBC$ the sides opposite equal angles are equal: $EB = EC$.

learning_objectives.label: Inscribed angles on arcs of equal measure; equal chords
learning_objectives.description: Corollary: in the same circle or in congruent circles, the measures of the inscribed angles subtended by arcs of equal measures are equal — and conversely, inscribed angles of equal measures subtend arcs of equal measures. Combine with 'equal chords cut equal arcs' to compare inscribed angles created by equal chords.

questions.stem: In the same circle or in congruent circles, the measures of the inscribed angles subtended by arcs of equal measures are …
solution: Corollary: in the same circle or in congruent circles, the measures of the inscribed angles subtended by arcs of equal measures are equal.
Reason: each inscribed angle equals half the measure of its subtended arc, and the two arcs have equal measures.

questions.stem: In circle M, $m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) = m(\overset{\frown}{DF})$, the inscribed angle $\angle ABC$ is subtended by $\overset{\frown}{AC}$ and the inscribed angle $\angle DEF$ is subtended by $\overset{\frown}{DF}$. If $m(\angle ABC) = 40°$ and $m(\angle DEF) = (3y - 5)°$, find the value of $y$.
solution: The inscribed angles subtended by arcs of equal measures are equal: $m(\angle DEF) = m(\angle ABC)$.

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ are two equal chords in a circle, and E is a point on $\overset{\frown}{BC}$ not containing A, where $m(\angle BEC) = 70°$. Find $m(\angle AEB)$ in degrees.
solution: $AB = AC$, so their arcs are equal in measure: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{AC})$ (equal chords cut arcs of equal measures).

$\angle AEB$ is inscribed on $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ and $\angle AEC$ is inscribed on $\overset{\frown}{AC}$; inscribed angles subtended by arcs of equal measures are equal, so $m(\angle AEB) = m(\angle AEC)$.
E lies on $\overset{\frown}{BC}$, so the ray $\overrightarrow{EA}$ falls between $\overrightarrow{EB}$ and $\overrightarrow{EC}$: $m(\angle AEB) + m(\angle AEC) = m(\angle BEC) = 70°$.
$2\,m(\angle AEB) = 70°$, so $m(\angle AEB) = 35°$.

questions.stem: ABC is a triangle inscribed in a circle where $AB = AC$ and $m(\angle BAC) = 40°$. Find $m(\overset{\frown}{AB})$ in degrees.
solution: $\angle BAC$ is an inscribed angle subtended by $\overset{\frown}{BC}$, so $m(\overset{\frown}{BC}) = 2 \times 40° = 80°$ (Corollary 1 of lesson 5-2).
$AB = AC$, and equal chords cut arcs of equal measures: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{AC})$.
The arcs make the whole circle: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) + m(\overset{\frown}{AC}) + m(\overset{\frown}{BC}) = 360°$, so $2\,m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 360° - 80° = 280°$.
$m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 140°$.

questions.stem: In the same circle or in congruent circles, the inscribed angles of equal measures subtend …
solution: This is the converse of the corollary, and it is true: in the same circle or in congruent circles, the inscribed angles of equal measures subtend arcs of equal measures.
Reason: each subtended arc measures double its inscribed angle, and doubling equal measures gives equal measures.

learning_objectives.label: The converse of Theorem 2: concyclic points
learning_objectives.description: Converse of Theorem 2: if two angles subtended to the same base and on the same side of it have the same measure, then their vertices are on an arc of a circle and the base is a chord in it. Use it to prove four points lie on one circle and to decide which quadrilaterals admit a circle through all four vertices.

questions.stem: If two angles subtended to the same base and on the same side of it have the same measure, then …
solution: Converse of Theorem 2: if two angles subtended to the same base and on the same side of it have the same measure, then their vertices are on an arc of a circle and the base is a chord in it.
This is the tool for proving that four points lie on one circle (concyclic points).

questions.stem: In $\triangle ABD$: $AB = AD$ and $m(\angle BAD) = 100°$. Find $m(\angle ADB)$ in degrees.
solution: $AB = AD$, so $\triangle ABD$ is isosceles and its base angles are equal: $m(\angle ADB) = m(\angle ABD)$.
$m(\angle ADB) = \dfrac{180° - m(\angle BAD)}{2} = \dfrac{180° - 100°}{2}$.
$m(\angle ADB) = 40°$.

questions.stem: Continuing: $AB = AD$, $m(\angle BAD) = 100°$, and C is a point on the same side of $\overline{AB}$ as D where $m(\angle ACB) = 40°$. Then …
solution: From the previous step, $m(\angle ADB) = \dfrac{180° - 100°}{2} = 40°$, so $m(\angle ACB) = m(\angle ADB) = 40°$.
$\angle ACB$ and $\angle ADB$ are both drawn on the base $\overline{AB}$ and on one side of it, with the same measure.
By the converse of Theorem 2, their vertices are on an arc of a circle in which $\overline{AB}$ is a chord: the points A, B, C and D have one circle passing through them.

questions.stem: A circle can be drawn passing through the four vertices of …
solution: In a rectangle ABCD, the diagonals are equal in length and bisect each other at their intersection point E.
So $EA = EB = EC = ED = \dfrac{1}{2}$ of a diagonal: E is equidistant from the four vertices.
The circle with center E and radius EA passes through the four vertices.

In a parallelogram or rhombus that is not a rectangle, the diagonals are not equal, so the intersection point is not equidistant from the four vertices — checking angles on a common base with the converse of Theorem 2 fails, and no such circle exists.

learning_objectives.label: The concept of the cyclic quadrilateral
learning_objectives.description: Define the cyclic quadrilateral as a quadrilateral figure whose four vertices belong to one circle, and identify whether a given figure is cyclic.

questions.stem: A cyclic quadrilateral is a quadrilateral figure whose four vertices …
solution: By definition (p.85): the cyclic quadrilateral "is a quadrilateral figure whose four vertices belong to one circle."
So all four vertices must lie on the same circle — three on a circle with the fourth elsewhere is not enough.

questions.stem: In a figure, the vertices A, B and C of quadrilateral ABCD lie on circle M, while the vertex D lies inside the circle. Is ABCD a cyclic quadrilateral?
solution: A cyclic quadrilateral is a quadrilateral figure whose four vertices belong to one circle (definition, p.85).
Here D lies inside circle M, not on it, so the four vertices do not belong to one circle.
$\therefore$ ABCD is not a cyclic quadrilateral.

questions.stem: PQRS is a square whose diagonals intersect at N. Which point is the center of the circle passing through the vertices P, Q, R and S?
solution: The diagonals of a square are equal in length and bisect each other at N.
$\therefore NP = NQ = NR = NS$, so the four vertices are at one distance from N.
$\therefore$ the circle with center N passing through P also passes through Q, R and S — every square is a cyclic quadrilateral (its four vertices belong to one circle, p.85).

questions.stem: ABCD is a quadrilateral whose diagonals intersect at E, $m(\angle ACB) = 54°$ and $m(\angle CED) = 92°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle DBC)$.
solution: $\angle CED$ is an exterior angle of triangle $EBC$ at E, because D, E, B lie on the diagonal $\overline{DB}$.
$\therefore m(\angle CED) = m(\angle EBC) + m(\angle ECB)$ (exterior angle of a triangle).
$\therefore 92° = m(\angle DBC) + 54°$
$\therefore m(\angle DBC) = 92° - 54° = 38°$

questions.stem: In the quadrilateral of the previous configuration, the diagonals of ABCD intersect at E with $m(\angle DBC) = 38°$ and $m(\angle DAC) = 38°$. Can a circle be drawn passing through the vertices of ABCD?
solution: $\angle DAC$ and $\angle DBC$ are two drawn angles on the base $\overline{DC}$ and in one direction of it, and $m(\angle DAC) = m(\angle DBC) = 38°$.
As in Lesson 5-4 (p.85): they are two equal drawn angles on the base and in one direction of it, so a circle can be drawn passing through the points D, C, B and A.
$\therefore$ ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

questions.stem: Which of the following quadrilaterals is certainly a cyclic quadrilateral?
solution: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal in length and bisect each other, so their intersection point is at one distance from the four vertices.
$\therefore$ the four vertices of a rectangle always belong to one circle — a rectangle is always a cyclic quadrilateral (definition, p.85).
A general parallelogram, rhombus or trapezium does not have its four vertices on one circle.

learning_objectives.label: Proving a quadrilateral is cyclic using equal angles on a base
learning_objectives.description: Prove a figure is a cyclic quadrilateral when two drawn angles on a base are equal in measure and in one direction of it, including the two-right-angles case where the base becomes a diameter.

questions.stem: Complete: if two drawn angles on a base are equal in measure and in one direction of it, then …
solution: This is the criterion used in Lesson 5-4 (p.85): two equal drawn angles on the base and in one direction of it mean a circle can be drawn passing through the two vertices of the angles and the two endpoints of the base.
$\therefore$ the four points belong to one circle, and the figure they form is a cyclic quadrilateral.

questions.stem: XYZL is a quadrilateral in which $m(\angle YXZ) = m(\angle YLZ) = 40°$, where X and L lie on the same side of $\overline{YZ}$. Why is XYZL a cyclic quadrilateral?
solution: $m(\angle YXZ) = m(\angle YLZ) = 40°$, and they are two drawn angles on the base $\overline{YZ}$ and in one direction of it.
As in Lesson 5-4 (p.85): a circle can be drawn passing through the points X, Y, Z and L.
i.e. the vertices of figure XYZL belong to one circle, so XYZL is a cyclic quadrilateral.

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter of circle M, X is the midpoint of the chord $\overline{AC}$, and ray $\overrightarrow{XM}$ intersects the tangent to the circle at B in the point Y. Find in degrees $m(\angle AXY) + m(\angle ABY)$.
solution: X is the midpoint of the chord $\overline{AC}$ $\therefore \overline{MX} \perp \overline{AC}$ (the segment from the center to the midpoint of a chord), so $m(\angle AXY) = 90°$.
$\overline{AB}$ is a diameter and $\overrightarrow{BY}$ is a tangent at B $\therefore \overrightarrow{BY} \perp \overline{AB}$, so $m(\angle ABY) = 90°$.
$\therefore m(\angle AXY) + m(\angle ABY) = 90° + 90° = 180°$
Note: since $m(\angle AXY) = m(\angle ABY) = 90°$ are two equal drawn angles on the base $\overline{AY}$ and in one direction of it, AXBY is a cyclic quadrilateral (Example 1, p.86).

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, $\overline{BD} \perp \overline{AC}$ at D and $\overline{CE} \perp \overline{AB}$ at E. Which of the following figures is a cyclic quadrilateral?
solution: $m(\angle BEC) = m(\angle BDC) = 90°$
They are two equal drawn angles on the base $\overline{BC}$ and in one direction of it (D and E are on the same side of $\overline{BC}$).
$\therefore$ a circle passes through B, C, D and E, so BCDE is a cyclic quadrilateral (Lesson 5-4 criterion, p.86).

questions.stem: In circle M, X and Y are the midpoints of the chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ respectively, and $m(\angle XMY) = 110°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle XAY)$.
solution: X is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ $\therefore \overline{MX} \perp \overline{AB}$, so $m(\angle AXM) = 90°$; similarly $m(\angle AYM) = 90°$.
In the quadrilateral AXMY the sum of the angle measures is $360°$.

questions.stem: In circle M, X and Y are the midpoints of the chords $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$. A circle passes through the points A, X, M and Y. Which segment is a diameter of that circle?
solution: $m(\angle AXM) = m(\angle AYM) = 90°$ (segment from the center to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it).
They are two equal drawn angles on the base $\overline{AM}$ and in one direction of it, so AXMY is a cyclic quadrilateral (Lesson 5-4, p.86).
The inscribed angle $\angle AXM = 90°$ must be subtended by a diameter, $\therefore \overline{AM}$ is a diameter of the circle passing through A, X, M and Y (as in the drill, p.87).

learning_objectives.label: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary (Theorem 3)
learning_objectives.description: State and apply Theorem 3: in a cyclic quadrilateral each two opposite angles are supplementary; compute missing angles, including algebraic and diameter configurations.

questions.stem: Complete: in a cyclic quadrilateral, each two opposite angles are …
solution: "In a cyclic quadrilateral, each two opposite angles are supplementary." (Theorem 3, p.88)
Supplementary means the sum of their measures is $180°$: $m(\angle A) + m(\angle C) = 180°$ and $m(\angle B) + m(\angle D) = 180°$.

questions.stem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral in which $m(\angle A) = 75°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle C)$.
solution: "In a cyclic quadrilateral, each two opposite angles are supplementary." (Theorem 3, p.88)
$\therefore m(\angle A) + m(\angle C) = 180°$
$\therefore m(\angle C) = 180° - 75° = 105°$

questions.stem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral in which $m(\angle B) = 98°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle D)$.
solution: "In a cyclic quadrilateral, each two opposite angles are supplementary." (Theorem 3, p.88)
$\therefore m(\angle B) + m(\angle D) = 180°$
$\therefore m(\angle D) = 180° - 98° = 82°$

questions.stem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral in which $m(\angle A) = 4y°$, $m(\angle C) = 108°$, $m(\angle B) = 5x°$ and $m(\angle D) = (2x + 40)°$. Find the value of $x$.
solution: "In a cyclic quadrilateral, each two opposite angles are supplementary." (Theorem 3, p.88)
$\therefore m(\angle B) + m(\angle D) = 180°$, i.e. $5x + 2x + 40 = 180$
$\therefore 7x = 140$, so $x = 20$
(Check with the other pair: $4y + 108 = 180 \Rightarrow y = 18$, so the data is consistent.)

questions.stem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral in which $m(\angle A) : m(\angle C) = 2 : 3$. Find in degrees $m(\angle A)$.
solution: "In a cyclic quadrilateral, each two opposite angles are supplementary." (Theorem 3, p.88) $\therefore m(\angle A) + m(\angle C) = 180°$
Let $m(\angle A) = 2k$ and $m(\angle C) = 3k$, then $2k + 3k = 180°$
$\therefore 5k = 180°$, so $k = 36°$ and $m(\angle A) = 2 \times 36° = 72°$

questions.stem: ABCD is a quadrilateral inscribed in circle M where $M \in \overline{AB}$, $CB = CD$ and $m(\angle BCD) = 132°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle ADC)$.
solution: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral $\therefore m(\angle A) + m(\angle BCD) = 180°$ "In a cyclic quadrilateral, each two opposite angles are supplementary." (Theorem 3, p.88)
$\therefore m(\angle A) = 180° - 132° = 48°$
Draw $\overline{BD}$: in triangle BCD, $CB = CD$ $\therefore m(\angle CDB) = m(\angle CBD) = \dfrac{180° - 132°}{2} = 24°$
$M \in \overline{AB}$ $\therefore \overline{AB}$ is a diameter of circle M $\therefore m(\angle ADB) = 90°$ (inscribed angle in a semicircle).
$\therefore m(\angle ADC) = m(\angle ADB) + m(\angle BDC) = 90° + 24° = 114°$

learning_objectives.label: Exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the opposite interior angle
learning_objectives.description: Apply the corollary of Theorem 3: the exterior angle at a vertex of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior angle at the opposite vertex.

questions.stem: Complete: the measure of the exterior angle at a vertex of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to …
solution: "The measure of the exterior angle at a vertex of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to the measure of the interior angle at the opposite vertex." (Corollary, p.90)

The exterior angle and the interior angle at the same vertex are supplementary, and the interior angle at the opposite vertex is also supplementary to it (Theorem 3) — the supplements of one angle are equal in measure.

questions.stem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, $E \in \overrightarrow{AB}$, $E \notin \overline{AB}$, and $m(\angle D) = 76°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle CBE)$.
solution: $\angle CBE$ is an exterior angle at the vertex B of the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, and $\angle D$ is the interior angle at the opposite vertex.
"The measure of the exterior angle at a vertex of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to the measure of the interior angle at the opposite vertex." (Corollary, p.90)
$\therefore m(\angle CBE) = m(\angle D) = 76°$

questions.stem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, $F \in \overrightarrow{CB}$, $F \notin \overline{CB}$, and $m(\angle ABF) = 95°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle ADC)$.
solution: $\angle ABF$ is an exterior angle at the vertex B of the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, and $\angle ADC$ is the interior angle at the opposite vertex D.
"The measure of the exterior angle at a vertex of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to the measure of the interior angle at the opposite vertex." (Corollary, p.90)
$\therefore m(\angle ADC) = m(\angle ABF) = 95°$

questions.stem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, $E \in \overrightarrow{AB}$, $E \notin \overline{AB}$, $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 100°$ and $m(\angle CBE) = 80°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle BDC)$.
solution: $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = 100°$ and $\angle ADB$ is an inscribed angle subtended by $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ $\therefore m(\angle ADB) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 100° = 50°$

$\angle CBE$ is an exterior angle at a vertex of the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD $\therefore m(\angle CBE) = m(\angle CDA) = 80°$ "The measure of the exterior angle at a vertex of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to the measure of the interior angle at the opposite vertex." (Corollary, p.90)
$\therefore m(\angle BDC) = m(\angle CDA) - m(\angle ADB) = 80° - 50° = 30°$

questions.stem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, $E \in \overrightarrow{BC}$, $E \notin \overline{BC}$, $m(\angle BAD) = 3x°$ and $m(\angle DCE) = (2x + 20)°$. Find the value of $x$.
solution: $\angle DCE$ is an exterior angle at the vertex C of the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, and $\angle BAD$ is the interior angle at the opposite vertex A.
"The measure of the exterior angle at a vertex of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to the measure of the interior angle at the opposite vertex." (Corollary, p.90) $\therefore 3x = 2x + 20$
$\therefore x = 20$

questions.stem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, $E \in \overrightarrow{AB}$, $E \notin \overline{AB}$, $m(\angle CBE) = 100°$ and in triangle ACD, $m(\angle CAD) = 35°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle ACD)$.
solution: $\angle CBE$ is an exterior angle at the vertex B of the cyclic quadrilateral ABCD $\therefore m(\angle ADC) = m(\angle CBE) = 100°$ "The measure of the exterior angle at a vertex of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to the measure of the interior angle at the opposite vertex." (Corollary, p.90)
In triangle ACD: $m(\angle ACD) = 180° - m(\angle ADC) - m(\angle CAD)$
$\therefore m(\angle ACD) = 180° - 100° - 35° = 45°$

learning_objectives.label: Proving a quadrilateral is cyclic (converse of Theorem 3)
learning_objectives.description: Prove a quadrilateral is cyclic using the converse of Theorem 3 (supplementary opposite angles) or its corollary (exterior angle equal to the opposite interior angle).

questions.stem: Complete: if two opposite angles of a quadrilateral are supplementary, then the quadrilateral is …
solution: "If two opposite angles of a quadrilateral are supplementary, then the quadrilateral is cyclic." (Converse of Theorem 3, p.90)
So checking that one pair of opposite angles adds up to $180°$ is enough to prove that a circle passes through the four vertices.

questions.stem: ABCD is a quadrilateral in which $m(\angle A) = 97°$ and $m(\angle C) = 83°$. Is ABCD a cyclic quadrilateral?
solution: $m(\angle A) + m(\angle C) = 97° + 83° = 180°$, so the two opposite angles A and C are supplementary.
"If two opposite angles of a quadrilateral are supplementary, then the quadrilateral is cyclic." (Converse of Theorem 3, p.90)
$\therefore$ ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

questions.stem: ABCD is a quadrilateral, $E \in \overrightarrow{AB}$, $E \notin \overline{AB}$, $m(\angle CBE) = 78°$ and $m(\angle ADC) = 78°$. What can you conclude?
solution: $\angle CBE$ is an exterior angle at the vertex B of the quadrilateral ABCD, and $\angle ADC$ is the interior angle at the opposite vertex D, and they are equal in measure.

"If the measure of the exterior angle at a vertex of a quadrilateral figure is equal to the measure of the interior angle at the opposite vertex, then the figure is a cyclic quadrilateral." (Corollary, p.91)
$\therefore$ ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

questions.stem: In quadrilateral ABCD the diagonal $\overline{AC}$ is drawn, $m(\angle DAC) = 40°$, $m(\angle CAB) = 35°$ and $m(\angle BCD) = 105°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle DAB) + m(\angle BCD)$, then decide whether ABCD is cyclic.
solution: $m(\angle DAB) = m(\angle DAC) + m(\angle CAB) = 40° + 35° = 75°$
$\therefore m(\angle DAB) + m(\angle BCD) = 75° + 105° = 180°$
"If two opposite angles of a quadrilateral are supplementary, then the quadrilateral is cyclic." (Converse of Theorem 3, p.90)
$\therefore$ ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral.

questions.stem: ABCD is a trapezium in which $\overline{AD} \parallel \overline{BC}$ and $m(\angle B) = m(\angle C) = 70°$ (an isosceles trapezium). Why is ABCD a cyclic quadrilateral?
solution: $\overline{AD} \parallel \overline{BC}$ and $\overline{AB}$ is a transversal $\therefore m(\angle A) + m(\angle B) = 180°$ (co-interior angles), so $m(\angle A) = 180° - 70° = 110°$
$\therefore m(\angle A) + m(\angle C) = 110° + 70° = 180°$: two opposite angles are supplementary.
"If two opposite angles of a quadrilateral are supplementary, then the quadrilateral is cyclic." (Converse of Theorem 3, p.90)
$\therefore$ every isosceles trapezium is a cyclic quadrilateral.

questions.stem: ABCD is a quadrilateral in which $m(\angle A) = 3x°$ and $m(\angle C) = (x + 60)°$. Find the value of $x$ which makes ABCD a cyclic quadrilateral.
solution: "If two opposite angles of a quadrilateral are supplementary, then the quadrilateral is cyclic." (Converse of Theorem 3, p.90) — so ABCD is cyclic when $m(\angle A) + m(\angle C) = 180°$.
$\therefore 4x = 120$, so $x = 30$
(Then $m(\angle A) = 90°$ and $m(\angle C) = 90°$, which are indeed supplementary.)

learning_objectives.label: Tangent segments from an external point (Theorem 4) and its corollaries
learning_objectives.description: Prove and apply Theorem 4: the two tangent segments drawn to a circle from an external point are equal in length; use the axis-of-symmetry and angle-bisection corollaries.

questions.stem: Complete: the two tangent segments drawn to a circle from a point outside it are …
solution: "The two tangent-segments drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length." (Theorem 4, p.93)

The proof (p.93-94): the two triangles ABM and ACM have $m(\angle B) = m(\angle C) = 90°$, $MB = MC$ (lengths of radii) and $\overline{AM}$ a common side, so $\triangle ABM \equiv \triangle ACM$ and $AB = AC$.

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ are two tangent segments to circle M at B and C, and $AB = 7$ cm. Find in cm the length of $\overline{AC}$.
solution: "The two tangent-segments drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length." (Theorem 4, p.93)
$\therefore AC = AB = 7$ cm

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ are two tangent segments to circle M at B and C, and $m(\angle BAC) = 48°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle BMC)$.
solution: $\overline{AB}$ is a tangent segment $\therefore \overline{MB} \perp \overline{AB}$, so $m(\angle ABM) = 90°$; similarly $m(\angle ACM) = 90°$.
In the quadrilateral ABMC the sum of the angle measures is $360°$.

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ are two tangent segments to circle M at B and C, and $m(\angle A) = 42°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle ABC)$.
solution: "The two tangent-segments drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length." (Theorem 4, p.93) $\therefore AB = AC$
$\therefore$ triangle ABC is isosceles, so $m(\angle ABC) = m(\angle ACB)$
$\therefore m(\angle ABC) = \dfrac{180° - 42°}{2} = 69°$

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ are two tangent segments to circle M at B and C, and $\overrightarrow{AM}$ intersects $\overline{BC}$ at D. If $BC = 9.6$ cm, find in cm the length of $\overline{BD}$.
solution: "The straight line passing through the center of the circle and the intersection point of the two tangents is an axis of symmetry to the chord of tangency of those two tangents." (Corollary 1, p.94)
$\therefore \overrightarrow{AM}$ is the axis of symmetry of the chord of tangency $\overline{BC}$, so $\overrightarrow{AM} \perp \overline{BC}$ and $BD = DC$.
$\therefore BD = \dfrac{9.6}{2} = 4.8$ cm

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{AC}$ are two tangent segments to circle M at B and C, and $m(\angle BMC) = 140°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle AMB)$.
solution: "The straight line passing through the center of the circle and the intersection point of its two tangents bisects the angle between these two tangents. It also bisects the angle between the two radii passing through the two points of tangency." (Corollary 2, p.94)
$\therefore \overrightarrow{MA}$ bisects $\angle BMC$, so $m(\angle AMB) = m(\angle AMC)$
$\therefore m(\angle AMB) = \dfrac{140°}{2} = 70°$

questions.stem: $\overrightarrow{XA}$ and $\overrightarrow{XB}$ are two tangents to a circle at A and B, $m(\angle AXB) = 64°$, and ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral in that circle with $m(\angle DCB) = 122°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle XAB)$, and hence show that $\overline{AB}$ bisects $\angle DAX$.
solution: $\overrightarrow{XA}$ and $\overrightarrow{XB}$ are two tangent segments "The two tangent-segments drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length." (Theorem 4, p.93) $\therefore XA = XB$
In triangle XAB: $m(\angle XAB) = m(\angle XBA) = \dfrac{180° - 64°}{2} = 58°$
ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral $\therefore m(\angle DAB) = 180° - m(\angle DCB) = 180° - 122° = 58°$ "In a cyclic quadrilateral, each two opposite angles are supplementary." (Theorem 3, p.88)
$\therefore m(\angle XAB) = m(\angle DAB) = 58°$, i.e. $\overline{AB}$ bisects $\angle DAX$.

learning_objectives.label: The inscribed circle of a polygon and common tangents of two circles
learning_objectives.description: Use the inscribed circle of a polygon (touching all sides internally) in perimeter/area problems, and identify and compute with common internal and external tangents of two circles.

questions.stem: Complete: the inscribed circle of a polygon is the circle which …
solution: "The inscribed circle of a polygon is the circle which touches all of its sides internally." (Definition, p.97)
i.e. the polygon is drawn outside the circle and each side touches the circle at exactly one point.

questions.stem: M is an inscribed circle of the quadrilateral ABCD with radius length $4$ cm, $AB = 8$ cm and $CD = 13$ cm. Find in cm the perimeter of ABCD.
solution: The circle touches the four sides, so the tangent segments drawn from each vertex are equal in length "The two tangent-segments drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length." (Theorem 4, p.93)
Adding the tangent segments as in Example 3 (p.98): $AB + CD = AD + BC = \dfrac{1}{2}$ the perimeter of ABCD.
$\therefore$ perimeter of ABCD $= 2 \times 21 = 42$ cm

questions.stem: M is an inscribed circle of the quadrilateral ABCD with radius length $6$ cm, $AB = 8$ cm and $CD = 15$ cm. Find in cm² the area of ABCD.
solution: As in Example 3 (p.98): $AB + CD = \dfrac{1}{2}$ the perimeter, so perimeter $= 2(8 + 15) = 46$ cm.
Area of ABCD $= \dfrac{1}{2} AB \times r + \dfrac{1}{2} BC \times r + \dfrac{1}{2} CD \times r + \dfrac{1}{2} AD \times r = \dfrac{1}{2}$ perimeter $\times r$
$\therefore$ Area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 46 \times 6 = 138$ cm²

questions.stem: The inscribed circle of triangle ABC touches its three sides, where $AB = 7$ cm, $BC = 8$ cm and $CA = 9$ cm. Find in cm the length of the tangent segment drawn from the vertex A.
solution: Let the tangent lengths from A, B, C be $p$, $q$, $r$. The two tangent segments from each vertex are equal "The two tangent-segments drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length." (Theorem 4, p.93)
$\therefore p + q = AB = 7$, $q + r = BC = 8$, $r + p = CA = 9$
Adding: $2(p + q + r) = 24$, so $p + q + r = 12$
$\therefore p = 12 - (q + r) = 12 - 8 = 4$ cm

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ is a common external tangent to the two circles M and N at A and B respectively, with radii lengths $10$ cm and $3$ cm, and $MN = 25$ cm. Find in cm the length of $\overline{AB}$.
solution: $\overline{MA} \perp \overline{AB}$ and $\overline{NB} \perp \overline{AB}$ (each radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of tangency).
Draw from N a segment parallel to $\overline{AB}$ meeting $\overline{MA}$ at F: then ABNF is a rectangle, $NF = AB$ and $MF = 10 - 3 = 7$ cm.
In the right triangle MFN: $NF = \sqrt{MN^2 - MF^2} = \sqrt{25^2 - 7^2} = \sqrt{625 - 49} = \sqrt{576} = 24$
$\therefore AB = 24$ cm

questions.stem: $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ is called a common internal tangent to the two circles M and N when …
solution: As on p.98: $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ is a common internal tangent to the two circles M and N because the two circles are located at two different sides of $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$.
If the two circles are located on the same side of the tangent line, it is a common external tangent.

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ is a tangent segment to circle M at B, the radius length is $6$ cm and $AB = 8$ cm. If $\overline{AM}$ intersects the circle at D where D lies between A and M, find in cm the length of $\overline{AD}$.
solution: $\overline{AB}$ is a tangent at B $\therefore \overline{MB} \perp \overline{AB}$, so triangle ABM is right-angled at B.
$\therefore AD = AM - MD = 10 - 6 = 4$ cm

learning_objectives.label: The angle of tangency and Theorem 5
learning_objectives.description: Define the angle of tangency (half the enclosed arc) and apply Theorem 5 and its corollary: it equals the inscribed angle, and half the central angle, subtended by the same arc.

questions.stem: The angle of tangency is the angle which is composed of the union of two rays, where …
solution: "The angle which is composed of the union of two rays, one is a tangent to the circle and the other contains a chord of the circle passing through the point of tangency." (Definition of the angle of tangency, p.100)
Its measure equals half the measure of the arc between its two sides: $m(\angle ABC) = \dfrac{1}{2} m(\overset{\frown}{AB})$.

questions.stem: $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is a tangent to a circle at B, $\overline{AB}$ is a chord in it, and the measure of the arc AB lying between the sides of $\angle ABC$ is $130°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle ABC)$.
solution: $\angle ABC$ is an angle of tangency "The angle which is composed of the union of two rays, one is a tangent to the circle and the other contains a chord of the circle passing through the point of tangency." (Definition of the angle of tangency, p.100)
The measure of the angle of tangency is half the measure of the arc between its two sides (p.100): $m(\angle ABC) = \dfrac{1}{2} m(\overset{\frown}{AB})$
$\therefore m(\angle ABC) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 130° = 65°$

questions.stem: $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is a tangent to a circle at B and $\overline{AB}$ is a chord in it. If the measure of the arc AB lying outside $\angle ABC$ is $210°$, find in degrees $m(\angle ABC)$.
solution: The whole circle measures $360°$, so the arc AB between the sides of $\angle ABC$ measures $360° - 210° = 150°$.
The measure of the angle of tangency is half the measure of the arc between its two sides (p.100).
$\therefore m(\angle ABC) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 150° = 75°$

questions.stem: $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter of circle M and $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is a tangent to the circle at B. Find in degrees $m(\angle ABC)$.
solution: $\overline{AB}$ is a diameter, so the arc AB between the sides of $\angle ABC$ is a semicircle of measure $180°$.
$m(\angle ABC) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 180° = 90°$
(This agrees with: the tangent at B is perpendicular to the diameter $\overline{AB}$.)

questions.stem: $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is a tangent to a circle at B, $\overline{AB}$ is a chord, and $m(\angle ABC) = 54°$. If D is a point on the arc AB lying outside $\angle ABC$, find in degrees $m(\angle ADB)$.
solution: $\angle ABC$ is an angle of tangency and $\angle ADB$ is an inscribed angle subtended by the same arc AB.
"The measure of the angle of tangency is equal to the measure of the inscribed angle subtended by the same arc." (Theorem 5, p.101)
$\therefore m(\angle ADB) = m(\angle ABC) = 54°$

questions.stem: $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is a tangent to circle M at B, $\overline{AB}$ is a chord of tangency, and $m(\angle ABC) = 62°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle MAB)$.
solution: "The measure of the angle of tangency is half the measure of the central angle subtended by the same arc." (Corollary, p.101) $\therefore m(\angle ABC) = \dfrac{1}{2} m(\angle AMB)$
$\therefore m(\angle AMB) = 2 \times 62° = 124°$
In triangle AMB: $MA = MB$ (lengths of radii), so it is isosceles.
$\therefore m(\angle MAB) = m(\angle MBA) = \dfrac{180° - 124°}{2} = 28°$

learning_objectives.label: Proving a ray is a tangent (converse of Theorem 5)
learning_objectives.description: Use the supplementary relation between the angle of tangency and the inscribed angle on its chord, and the converse of Theorem 5 to prove a ray is a tangent to a circle.

questions.stem: A ray is drawn from one end of a chord of a circle so that the angle between this ray and the chord is equal in measure to the inscribed angle subtended by the chord in the alternate side. Then this ray is …
solution: "If a ray is drawn from one end of a chord of a circle so that the angle between this ray and the chord is equal in measure to the inscribed angle subtended by the chord in the alternate side, then this ray is a tangent to this circle." (Converse of Theorem 5, p.103)
This is the tool used to prove that a given ray or line touches a circle without knowing its center.

questions.stem: $\overrightarrow{BC}$ is a tangent to a circle at B, $\overline{AB}$ is a chord, and $m(\angle ABC) = 68°$. If E is a point on the arc AB lying between the sides of $\angle ABC$, find in degrees $m(\angle AEB)$.
solution: "The angle of tangency is supplementary to the drawn inscribed angle on the chord of the angle of tangency and in one side of it." (Important notice, p.102)
$\angle AEB$ is the inscribed angle drawn on the chord $\overline{AB}$ and in one side of the angle of tangency $\angle ABC$.
$\therefore m(\angle AEB) = 180° - m(\angle ABC) = 180° - 68° = 112°$

questions.stem: ABC is a triangle inscribed in a circle. A ray $\overrightarrow{AD}$ is drawn where D and C are on opposite sides of $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$, with $m(\angle DAB) = 62°$ and $m(\angle ACB) = 62°$. What can you conclude?
solution: $\angle DAB$ is the angle between the ray $\overrightarrow{AD}$ and the chord $\overline{AB}$, and $\angle ACB$ is the inscribed angle subtended by $\overline{AB}$ in the alternate side, and they are equal in measure ($62°$).

"If a ray is drawn from one end of a chord of a circle so that the angle between this ray and the chord is equal in measure to the inscribed angle subtended by the chord in the alternate side, then this ray is a tangent to this circle." (Converse of Theorem 5, p.103)
$\therefore \overrightarrow{AD}$ is a tangent to the circle at A.

questions.stem: In triangle ABC, $m(\angle BAC) = 50°$ and $m(\angle ABC) = 60°$. A ray $\overrightarrow{AD}$ is drawn on the opposite side of $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ from C. Find in degrees the measure of $\angle DAB$ which makes $\overrightarrow{AD}$ a tangent to the circle passing through the vertices of the triangle.
solution: In triangle ABC: $m(\angle ACB) = 180° - 50° - 60° = 70°$

"If a ray is drawn from one end of a chord of a circle so that the angle between this ray and the chord is equal in measure to the inscribed angle subtended by the chord in the alternate side, then this ray is a tangent to this circle." (Converse of Theorem 5, p.103)
$\angle ACB$ is the inscribed angle subtended by the chord $\overline{AB}$ in the alternate side of $\overrightarrow{AD}$.
$\therefore \overrightarrow{AD}$ is a tangent when $m(\angle DAB) = m(\angle ACB) = 70°$

questions.stem: ABC is a triangle inscribed in a circle, $\overrightarrow{AD}$ is a tangent to the circle at A, $X \in \overline{AB}$ and $Y \in \overline{AC}$ where $\overline{XY} \parallel \overline{BC}$, and $m(\angle ACB) = 48°$. Find in degrees $m(\angle AYX)$, and hence deduce that $\overrightarrow{AD}$ is a tangent to the circle passing through A, X and Y.
solution: $\overline{XY} \parallel \overline{BC}$ and $\overline{AC}$ is a transversal $\therefore m(\angle AYX) = m(\angle ACB) = 48°$ (corresponding angles).

$\overrightarrow{AD}$ is a tangent and $\overline{AB}$ is the chord of tangency $\therefore m(\angle DAB) = m(\angle ACB) = 48°$ "The measure of the angle of tangency is equal to the measure of the inscribed angle subtended by the same arc." (Theorem 5, p.101)
$\therefore m(\angle DAX) = m(\angle AYX) = 48°$
By the converse of Theorem 5 (p.103), $\overrightarrow{AD}$ is a tangent to the circle passing through the points A, X and Y (Example 4, p.103).

questions.stem: ABC is a triangle inscribed in a circle, $\overrightarrow{BD}$ is a tangent to the circle at B, $X \in \overline{AB}$ and $Y \in \overline{BC}$ where $\overline{XY} \parallel \overrightarrow{BD}$. Then the figure AXYC is …
