solution: $\overrightarrow{BD}$ is a tangent at B and $\overline{AB}$ is a chord of tangency $\therefore m(\angle DBA) = m(\angle ACB)$ "The measure of the angle of tangency is equal to the measure of the inscribed angle subtended by the same arc." (Theorem 5, p.101)
$\overline{XY} \parallel \overrightarrow{BD}$ and $\overline{AB}$ intersects both of them $\therefore m(\angle BXY) = m(\angle DBA)$, so $m(\angle BXY) = m(\angle ACB)$.
$\angle BXY$ is an exterior angle at the vertex X of the quadrilateral XYCA, equal to the interior angle at the opposite vertex C.

"If the measure of the exterior angle at a vertex of a quadrilateral figure is equal to the measure of the interior angle at the opposite vertex, then the figure is a cyclic quadrilateral." (Corollary, p.91)
$\therefore$ AXYC is a cyclic quadrilateral (Example 1, p.102).

learning_objectives.label: First-degree equations in two variables
learning_objectives.description: Identify an equation of first degree in two variables; find ordered-pair solutions; represent the infinite solution set by a straight line.

questions.stem: Which of the following ordered pairs is a solution of the equation $x + y = 12$?
solution: A solution of a first-degree equation in two variables is an ordered pair $(x, y)$ that satisfies the equation.
Test $(5, 7)$: $5 + 7 = 12$ ✓, so it is a solution.
The other pairs give $4 + 9 = 13$, $6 + 7 = 13$ and $3 + 8 = 11$, none of which equals $12$.

questions.stem: In the equation $2x - y = 5$, if $x = 4$ then $y = \dots$
solution: Substitute $x = 4$ into the equation: $2(4) - y = 5$.
So $8 - y = 5$, which gives $y = 8 - 5 = 3$.
Therefore $(4, 3)$ is a solution of the equation.

questions.stem: If the ordered pair $(k, 2k)$ is a solution of the equation $x + y = 9$, find the value of $k$.
solution: Since $(k, 2k)$ is a solution, substitute $x = k$ and $y = 2k$: $k + 2k = 9$.
Therefore $k = 3$ (the solution is the ordered pair $(3, 6)$).

questions.stem: For a first-degree equation in two variables, where $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, the number of solutions is $\dots$
solution: For every real value of $x$ we can compute a corresponding $y$, so each choice of $x$ gives one solution $(x, y)$.
Since $x$ can be any real number, the substitution set is $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ and there is an infinite number of solutions.
Graphically: every point of the straight line representing the equation is a solution.

questions.stem: If $(a, a - 4)$ is a solution of the equation $3x - y = 16$, find the value of $a$.
solution: Substitute $x = a$ and $y = a - 4$ into the equation: $3a - (a - 4) = 16$.
Then $2a = 12$, so $a = 6$ (the solution is $(6, 2)$: check $3(6) - 2 = 16$ ✓).

learning_objectives.label: Graphical solution of two first-degree equations
learning_objectives.description: Solve two first-degree equations graphically as the intersection point of two lines; recognize parallel lines (no solution) and coincident lines (infinitely many solutions).

questions.stem: The two straight lines $L_1: y = x + 1$ and $L_2: y = -x + 5$ intersect at the point $\dots$
solution: At the intersection point the two equations hold together, so $x + 1 = -x + 5$.
Then $2x = 4$, so $x = 2$.
Substituting in $L_1$: $y = 2 + 1 = 3$, so $L_1 \cap L_2 = \{(2, 3)\}$.

questions.stem: The number of common solutions of the two equations $2x + y = 4$ and $4x + 2y = 6$ is $\dots$
solution: Divide the second equation by $2$: $2x + y = 3$.
The two lines have the same slope ($y = -2x + 4$ and $y = -2x + 3$) but different $y$-intercepts, so $L_1 \parallel L_2$.
Since $L_1 \cap L_2 = \varnothing$, there is no common solution.

questions.stem: The two equations $3x - y = 2$ and $6x - 2y = 4$ represent $\dots$
solution: Multiply the first equation by $2$: $6x - 2y = 4$, which is exactly the second equation.
So the two equations represent the same straight line: two coincident lines.
Every point of the line is a common solution, so there is an infinite number of common solutions.

questions.stem: The two straight lines $y = 2x$ and $x + y = 6$ intersect at a point. Find the $x$-coordinate of this point.
solution: At the intersection point both equations hold, so substitute $y = 2x$ into $x + y = 6$: $x + 2x = 6$.
So $3x = 6$, giving $x = 2$.
(Then $y = 2(2) = 4$: the intersection point is $(2, 4)$.)

questions.stem: If the two equations $2x + y = 7$ and $6x + 3y = k$ represent two coincident straight lines, then $k = \dots$
solution: Two coincident lines have proportional equations: multiplying $2x + y = 7$ by $3$ gives $6x + 3y = 21$.
For the second equation to be the same line, $k = 21$.
Then every solution of the first equation is a solution of the second (infinitely many common solutions).

learning_objectives.label: Algebraic solution of two first-degree equations
learning_objectives.description: Solve two simultaneous first-degree equations by the substitution method and the omitting (elimination) method.

questions.stem: Solve algebraically the two equations $x + y = 10$ and $x - y = 4$, then find the value of $x$.
solution: Use the omitting method: add the two equations to omit $y$: $(x + y) + (x - y) = 10 + 4$.
So $2x = 14$, giving $x = 7$.
Substituting in the first equation: $7 + y = 10$, so $y = 3$; the solution set is $\{(7, 3)\}$.

questions.stem: The solution set of the two equations $2x - y = 1$ and $x + 2y = 8$ is $\dots$
solution: Substitution method: from the first equation $y = 2x - 1$.
Substitute in the second: $x + 2(2x - 1) = 8$, so $5x - 2 = 8$, then $5x = 10$ and $x = 2$.
Substituting back: $y = 2(2) - 1 = 3$, so the solution set is $\{(2, 3)\}$.

questions.stem: If $3x + 2y = 12$ and $x = y + 4$, find the value of $x + y$.
solution: Substitute $x = y + 4$ into the first equation: $3(y + 4) + 2y = 12$.

questions.stem: Solve the two equations $3x + 4y = 10$ and $5x - 2y = 8$, then find the value of $xy$.
solution: Multiply the second equation by $2$: $10x - 4y = 16$.
Add it to the first equation to omit $y$: $13x = 26$, so $x = 2$.
Substitute in $5x - 2y = 8$: $10 - 2y = 8$, so $y = 1$; therefore $xy = 2 \times 1 = 2$.

learning_objectives.label: Applications on simultaneous first-degree equations
learning_objectives.description: Use systems of first-degree equations in applications: unknown coefficients, digit problems, sum-and-difference problems.

questions.stem: The sum of two numbers is 15 and their difference is 3. Find the larger number.
solution: Let the two numbers be $x$ and $y$ with $x > y$: then $x + y = 15$ and $x - y = 3$.
Adding the two equations: $2x = 18$, so $x = 9$.
Substituting: $y = 15 - 9 = 6$; the larger number is $9$.

questions.stem: If $(2, 1)$ is the solution of the two equations $ax + by = 7$ and $ax - by = 1$, find the value of $a + b$.
solution: Since $(2, 1)$ satisfies both equations: $2a + b = 7$ and $2a - b = 1$.
Adding the two equations: $4a = 8$, so $a = 2$.
Substituting in $2a + b = 7$: $4 + b = 7$, so $b = 3$; therefore $a + b = 5$.

questions.stem: A two-digit number: the sum of its digits is 9. If the two digits are reversed, the resulting number is 27 more than the original number. What is the original number?
solution: Let the units digit be $x$ and the tens digit be $y$: then $x + y = 9$ … (1), and the value of the number is $x + 10y$.
After reversing, the value is $y + 10x$; given $(y + 10x) - (x + 10y) = 27$, so $9x - 9y = 27$; dividing by $9$: $x - y = 3$ … (2).
The original number is $x + 10y = 6 + 30 = 36$ (check: $63 - 36 = 27$ ✓).

questions.stem: The perimeter of a rectangle is 26 cm and its length exceeds its width by 3 cm. The area of the rectangle $= \dots$ cm$^2$.
solution: Let the length be $x$ and the width be $y$: the perimeter gives $2(x + y) = 26$, so $x + y = 13$, and $x - y = 3$.
The area $= x \times y = 8 \times 5 = 40$ cm$^2$.

learning_objectives.label: Graphical solution of a second-degree equation
learning_objectives.description: Solve ax²+bx+c=0 graphically: the roots are the x-coordinates of the intersection points of the curve of f(x)=ax²+bx+c with the x-axis (two, one, or no points).

questions.stem: The curve of the function $f(x) = x^2 - 5x + 6$ cuts the x-axis at the two points $(2, 0)$ and $(3, 0)$. The solution set of the equation $x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0$ is $\dots$
solution: The roots of $f(x) = 0$ are the x-coordinates of the points where the curve of $f$ intersects the x-axis.
The curve cuts the x-axis at $(2, 0)$ and $(3, 0)$, so the roots are $2$ and $3$.
Therefore the solution set is $\{2, 3\}$.

questions.stem: To solve the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ graphically, we draw the curve of $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ and take the $x$-coordinates of its points of intersection with $\dots$
solution: By definition, the solutions of $f(x) = 0$ are the values of $x$ at which the function equals zero.
On the graph these are exactly the points where the curve meets the x-axis ($y = 0$).
So we identify the set of x-coordinates of the intersection points of the curve with the x-axis.

questions.stem: The curve of $f(x) = x^2 + 2x + 1$ touches the x-axis at one point only. The solution set of the equation $x^2 + 2x + 1 = 0$ is $\dots$
solution: Factorize: $x^2 + 2x + 1 = (x + 1)^2$, so the curve touches the x-axis where $(x + 1)^2 = 0$.
That happens only at $x = -1$, i.e. at the single point $(-1, 0)$.
So the solution set is $\{-1\}$ (one repeated root).

questions.stem: The curve of $f(x) = x^2 + 4$ lies completely above the x-axis. The solution set of the equation $x^2 + 4 = 0$ in $\mathbb{R}$ is $\dots$
solution: The curve does not intersect the x-axis at any point, so there is no real $x$ with $f(x) = 0$.
Algebraically: $x^2 = -4$ has no solution in $\mathbb{R}$ because $x^2 \geq 0$ for every real $x$.
So the solution set is $\varnothing$.

learning_objectives.label: The general rule (quadratic formula)
learning_objectives.description: Solve ax²+bx+c=0 algebraically using x = (-b ± √(b²-4ac))/2a; approximate irrational roots; recognize ∅ when b²-4ac < 0; applications.

questions.stem: Using the general rule, solve the equation $x^2 - 5x + 4 = 0$, then find the larger root.
solution: $x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} = \dfrac{5 \pm 3}{2}$.
So $x = 4$ or $x = 1$; the solution set is $\{1, 4\}$ and the larger root is $4$.

questions.stem: Find the positive root of the equation $2x^2 = 3x + 2$.
solution: Put the equation in the general form: $2x^2 - 3x - 2 = 0$, so $a = 2$, $b = -3$, $c = -2$.
So $x = 2$ or $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$; the positive root is $2$.

questions.stem: Solve the equation $3x^2 - 7x + 1 = 0$ rounding the results to two decimal places, then give the larger root.
solution: $x = \dfrac{7 \pm \sqrt{37}}{6} = \dfrac{7 \pm 6.08}{6}$ (since $\sqrt{37} \approx 6.08$).
So $x \approx \dfrac{13.08}{6} \approx 2.18$ or $x \approx \dfrac{0.92}{6} \approx 0.15$; the larger root $\approx 2.18$.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown so that its path follows the relation $y = -x^2 + 4x + 5$, where $x$ is the horizontal distance in metres and $y$ is the height above the ground. Find the horizontal distance at which the ball reaches the ground ($y = 0$).
solution: Put $y = 0$: $-x^2 + 4x + 5 = 0$; multiplying both sides by $-1$: $x^2 - 4x - 5 = 0$.
Factorize (or use the rule): $(x - 5)(x + 1) = 0$, so $x = 5$ or $x = -1$.
$x = -1$ is refused because a horizontal distance cannot be negative; the ball lands at $x = 5$ metres.

questions.stem: The solution set of the equation $x^2 + 2x + 5 = 0$ in $\mathbb{R}$ is $\dots$
solution: Since $b^2 - 4ac < 0$, the expression $\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} \notin \mathbb{R}$.
So the equation has no real roots and the solution set is $\varnothing$.

learning_objectives.label: Systems of one first-degree and one second-degree equation
learning_objectives.description: Solve two equations in two variables, one of first degree and one of second degree, by substituting from the linear equation into the quadratic one.

questions.stem: The solution set of the two equations $x + y = 5$ and $xy = 6$ is $\dots$
solution: From the first-degree equation: $y = 5 - x$; substitute in the second-degree equation: $x(5 - x) = 6$.
When $x = 2$, $y = 3$; when $x = 3$, $y = 2$; the solution set is $\{(2, 3), (3, 2)\}$.

questions.stem: Solve the two equations $y = x - 3$ and $x^2 + y^2 = 5$, then find the sum of the $x$-values of the solutions.
solution: Substitute $y = x - 3$ into $x^2 + y^2 = 5$: $x^2 + (x - 3)^2 = 5$.
$(x - 1)(x - 2) = 0$, so $x = 1$ or $x = 2$ (solutions $(1, -2)$ and $(2, -1)$); the sum of the $x$-values is $1 + 2 = 3$.

questions.stem: If $x + y = 8$ and $x^2 - y^2 = 32$, find the value of $xy$.
solution: Factorize the second equation: $x^2 - y^2 = (x + y)(x - y) = 32$.
Adding $x + y = 8$ and $x - y = 4$: $2x = 12$, so $x = 6$ and $y = 2$; therefore $xy = 12$.

questions.stem: The solution set of the two equations $y = 2x + 1$ and $y = x^2 - 2$ is $\dots$
solution: At a common solution: $x^2 - 2 = 2x + 1$, so $x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0$.
Factorize: $(x - 3)(x + 1) = 0$, so $x = 3$ or $x = -1$.

learning_objectives.label: Applications on first- and second-degree systems
learning_objectives.description: Use mixed-degree systems in applications such as rectangle perimeter-and-area problems and sum-and-product number problems.

questions.stem: A rectangle has a perimeter of 20 cm and an area of 24 cm$^2$. Find its length (the longer dimension) in cm.
solution: Let the dimensions be $x$ and $y$: the perimeter gives $2(x + y) = 20$, so $x + y = 10$, i.e. $y = 10 - x$; the area gives $xy = 24$.
So $x = 6$ or $x = 4$: the dimensions are $6$ cm and $4$ cm, and the length is $6$ cm.

questions.stem: Two positive numbers: their sum is 13 and their product is 40. Find the larger number.
solution: Let the numbers be $x$ and $y$: $x + y = 13$, so $y = 13 - x$, and $xy = 40$.
So $x = 8$ or $x = 5$: the two numbers are $8$ and $5$, and the larger is $8$.

questions.stem: The sum of two numbers is 9 and the sum of their squares is 45. Find the product of the two numbers.
solution: Let the numbers be $x$ and $y$: $x + y = 9$ and $x^2 + y^2 = 45$.
Square the first equation: $(x + y)^2 = x^2 + y^2 + 2xy = 81$.
So $45 + 2xy = 81$, giving $2xy = 36$ and $xy = 18$ (the numbers are $6$ and $3$).

questions.stem: A rectangle has a perimeter of 28 cm and an area of 48 cm$^2$. Its dimensions are $\dots$
solution: Let the dimensions be $x$ and $y$: $2(x + y) = 28$, so $x + y = 14$, and $xy = 48$.
So $x = 8$ or $x = 6$: the dimensions are $8$ cm and $6$ cm (check: perimeter $28$ ✓, area $48$ ✓).

learning_objectives.label: Set of zeroes of a polynomial function
learning_objectives.description: Find Z(f), the set of values of x for which f(x)=0, for polynomial functions; Z(f) may be empty, finite, or R.

questions.stem: If $f(x) = 3x - 6$, then $Z(f) = \dots$
solution: So $3x = 6$, giving $x = 2$.
Therefore $Z(f) = \{2\}$.

questions.stem: If $f(x) = x^2 - 16$, then $Z(f) = \dots$
solution: So $x = \pm 4$.
Therefore $Z(f) = \{-4, 4\}$.

questions.stem: If $f(x) = 7$ for every real $x$, then $Z(f) = \dots$
solution: $f$ is a constant function whose value is always $7$.
There is no real number $x$ that makes $f(x) = 0$.
Therefore $Z(f) = \varnothing$.

questions.stem: If $f(x) = x^2 + 9$, then $Z(f) = \dots$
solution: Since $x^2 \geq 0$ for every real $x$, no real number satisfies this: $x = \pm\sqrt{-9} \notin \mathbb{R}$.
Therefore $Z(f) = \varnothing$.

questions.stem: If $f(x) = x^3 - 5x^2 + 6x$, find the sum of the elements of $Z(f)$.
solution: Put $f(x) = 0$: $x^3 - 5x^2 + 6x = 0$; take $x$ as a common factor: $x(x^2 - 5x + 6) = 0$.
Factorize the bracket: $x(x - 2)(x - 3) = 0$, so $x = 0$, $x = 2$ or $x = 3$.
$Z(f) = \{0, 2, 3\}$ and the sum of its elements $= 0 + 2 + 3 = 5$.

learning_objectives.label: Algebraic fractional function and its domain
learning_objectives.description: Define n(x)=p(x)/f(x) for polynomials p, f; the domain is R minus the set of zeroes of the denominator.

questions.stem: The domain of the algebraic fractional function $n(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 5}$ is $\dots$
solution: The domain of an algebraic fractional function is $\mathbb{R}$ minus the set of zeroes of the denominator.
Put $x - 5 = 0$: the zero of the denominator is $x = 5$.
Therefore the domain of $n$ is $\mathbb{R} - \{5\}$.

questions.stem: The domain of $n(x) = \dfrac{x + 1}{x^2 - 9}$ is $\dots$
solution: The domain is $\mathbb{R}$ minus the set of zeroes of the denominator $x^2 - 9$.
Therefore the domain of $n$ is $\mathbb{R} - \{-3, 3\}$.

questions.stem: The domain of $n(x) = \dfrac{x^2 + 1}{x^2 - 4x}$ is $\dots$
solution: Only the zeroes of the denominator matter for the domain (the numerator $x^2 + 1$ has no real zeroes, but that does not affect the domain).
Therefore the domain of $n$ is $\mathbb{R} - \{0, 4\}$.

questions.stem: If $n(x) = \dfrac{x + 4}{x - 2}$, find $n(4)$.
solution: The domain of $n$ is $\mathbb{R} - \{2\}$, and $4$ belongs to the domain, so $n(4)$ exists.

questions.stem: If the domain of the function $n(x) = \dfrac{x - 1}{x^2 - ax + 16}$ is $\mathbb{R} - \{4\}$, find the value of $a$.
solution: The domain excludes only $x = 4$, so $4$ is the only zero of the denominator: $x^2 - ax + 16 = (x - 4)^2$.
Expanding: $(x - 4)^2 = x^2 - 8x + 16$; comparing coefficients gives $a = 8$.
Check: substituting $x = 4$ in $x^2 - 8x + 16$ gives $16 - 32 + 16 = 0$ ✓, and it is the only zero.

learning_objectives.label: Common domain of algebraic fractions
learning_objectives.description: Find the common domain of two or more algebraic fractions: R minus the union of the sets of zeroes of all denominators.

questions.stem: The common domain of the two algebraic fractions $n_1(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 2}$ and $n_2(x) = \dfrac{3}{x + 5}$ is $\dots$
solution: The common domain $= \mathbb{R} -$ (the set of zeroes of the two denominators).
Zero of $x - 2$ is $2$; zero of $x + 5$ is $-5$.
Therefore the common domain is $\mathbb{R} - \{-5, 2\}$.

questions.stem: The common domain of $n_1(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}$ and $n_2(x) = \dfrac{2}{x^2 - 1}$ is $\dots$
solution: Zeroes of the first denominator: $x = 0$.
Zeroes of the second denominator: $x^2 - 1 = 0$, so $x = \pm 1$.
The common domain $= \mathbb{R} -$ (union of the zeroes) $= \mathbb{R} - \{-1, 0, 1\}$.

questions.stem: The common domain of $n_1(x) = \dfrac{3}{x^2 - x}$ and $n_2(x) = \dfrac{5}{x - 1}$ is $\dots$
solution: Zeroes of the first denominator: $x^2 - x = x(x - 1) = 0$, so $x = 0$ or $x = 1$.
Zeroes of the second denominator: $x = 1$.
The union of the zeroes is $\{0, 1\}$, so the common domain is $\mathbb{R} - \{0, 1\}$.

questions.stem: If $n_1(x) = \dfrac{-7}{x + 3}$ and $n_2(x) = \dfrac{x}{x - k}$, and the common domain of $n_1, n_2$ is $\mathbb{R} - \{-3, 6\}$, find the value of $k$.
solution: The zero of the first denominator is $x = -3$, which accounts for the excluded value $-3$.
So the other excluded value $6$ must be the zero of the second denominator: $x - k = 0$ at $x = 6$.
Therefore $k = 6$.

learning_objectives.label: Reducing an algebraic fraction
learning_objectives.description: Factorize numerator and denominator, identify the domain BEFORE cancelling, then remove common factors to reach the simplest form.

questions.stem: For $x \neq -5$, the simplest form of $\dfrac{x^2 - 25}{x + 5}$ is $\dots$
solution: Factorize the numerator: $x^2 - 25 = (x - 5)(x + 5)$.
The domain excludes $x = -5$ (the zero of the denominator), so we may cancel the common factor $(x + 5)$.
The simplest form is $x - 5$.

questions.stem: The simplest form of $n(x) = \dfrac{x^2 + 3x}{x^2 - 9}$ is $\dots$
solution: Factorize: $n(x) = \dfrac{x(x + 3)}{(x - 3)(x + 3)}$.
Identify the domain before cancelling: $\mathbb{R} - \{-3, 3\}$.
Cancel the common factor $(x + 3)$: the simplest form is $\dfrac{x}{x - 3}$.

questions.stem: The domain of $n(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x^2 - x - 2}$ is $\dots$
solution: The domain must be identified from the ORIGINAL denominator, before any cancelling.
Therefore the domain is $\mathbb{R} - \{-1, 2\}$ (even though the fraction reduces to $\dfrac{x + 2}{x + 1}$).

questions.stem: If $n(x) = \dfrac{x^3 + 2x^2 - 3x}{x^3 - x}$, reduce $n$ to its simplest form showing the domain, then find $n(3)$.
solution: Factorize: numerator $= x(x^2 + 2x - 3) = x(x + 3)(x - 1)$; denominator $= x(x^2 - 1) = x(x - 1)(x + 1)$.
The domain of $n$ is $\mathbb{R} - \{-1, 0, 1\}$ (zeroes of the original denominator).
Cancel the common factors $x$ and $(x - 1)$: $n(x) = \dfrac{x + 3}{x + 1}$.

questions.stem: If the simplest form of the algebraic fraction $n(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 6x + 9}{x^2 - a}$ is $\dfrac{x - 3}{x + 3}$, then $a = \dots$
solution: Factorize the numerator: $x^2 - 6x + 9 = (x - 3)^2$.
For the fraction to reduce to $\dfrac{x - 3}{x + 3}$, the denominator must be $(x - 3)(x + 3) = x^2 - 9$.
Comparing $x^2 - a$ with $x^2 - 9$ gives $a = 9$.

learning_objectives.label: Equality of two algebraic fractions
learning_objectives.description: Two algebraic fractions are equal iff they have the same domain and equal values at every x of that domain; same simplest form with different domains is NOT equality.

questions.stem: Two algebraic fractions $n_1$ and $n_2$ are equal ($n_1 = n_2$) if $\dots$
solution: By definition, $n_1 = n_2$ requires TWO conditions together.
First: the domain of $n_1$ $=$ the domain of $n_2$; second: $n_1(x) = n_2(x)$ for each $x$ in that domain.
Having the same simplest form alone is not enough — the domains must also coincide.

questions.stem: If $n_1(x) = \dfrac{x + 2}{x^2 - 4}$ and $n_2(x) = \dfrac{1}{x - 2}$, which of the following is correct?
solution: Reduce $n_1$: $n_1(x) = \dfrac{x + 2}{(x - 2)(x + 2)} = \dfrac{1}{x - 2}$, with domain $\mathbb{R} - \{-2, 2\}$.
$n_2$ has the same simplest form but its domain is $\mathbb{R} - \{2\}$.
Since the domains are different, $n_1 \neq n_2$ (although $n_1(x) = n_2(x)$ on the common domain $\mathbb{R} - \{-2, 2\}$).

questions.stem: If $n_1(x) = \dfrac{3x}{3x + 6}$ and $n_2(x) = \dfrac{x}{x + 2}$, which of the following is correct?
solution: Reduce $n_1$: $n_1(x) = \dfrac{3x}{3(x + 2)} = \dfrac{x}{x + 2}$, with domain $\mathbb{R} - \{-2\}$.
$n_2$ has the same simplest form and the same domain $\mathbb{R} - \{-2\}$.
Both equality conditions hold, so $n_1 = n_2$.

questions.stem: If $n_1(x) = \dfrac{1 + a}{x - 5}$ and $n_2(x) = \dfrac{9}{x - 5}$, and $n_1 = n_2$, find the value of $a$.
solution: The two fractions already have the same domain $\mathbb{R} - \{5\}$.
For $n_1(x) = n_2(x)$ at every $x$ of the domain, the numerators must be equal: $1 + a = 9$.
Therefore $a = 8$.

learning_objectives.label: Adding and subtracting algebraic fractions
learning_objectives.description: Add/subtract algebraic fractions over the common domain using a common denominator (L.C.M. of denominators), then reduce.

questions.stem: For $x \neq 1$: $\dfrac{3}{x - 1} + \dfrac{2}{x - 1} = \dots$
solution: The two fractions have the same denominator $(x - 1)$.
Add the numerators over the common denominator: $\dfrac{3 + 2}{x - 1}$.
So the sum $= \dfrac{5}{x - 1}$ on the domain $\mathbb{R} - \{1\}$.

questions.stem: In the simplest form: $\dfrac{x}{x - 2} - \dfrac{x}{x + 2} = \dots$
solution: The common domain is $\mathbb{R} - \{-2, 2\}$ and the L.C.M. of the denominators is $(x - 2)(x + 2)$.

questions.stem: The domain of $n(x) = \dfrac{3}{x + 2} + \dfrac{x + 2}{x^2 + 2x}$ is $\dots$
solution: Factorize the second denominator: $x^2 + 2x = x(x + 2)$, with zeroes $\{-2, 0\}$.
The first denominator's zero is $-2$.
The domain of the sum is $\mathbb{R}$ minus the zeroes of both denominators: $\mathbb{R} - \{-2, 0\}$.

questions.stem: If $n(x) = \dfrac{5}{x - 4} + \dfrac{4}{4 - x}$, find $n(6)$.
solution: Write the second fraction with denominator $(x - 4)$: $\dfrac{4}{4 - x} = \dfrac{-4}{x - 4}$.
So $n(x) = \dfrac{5}{x - 4} - \dfrac{4}{x - 4} = \dfrac{1}{x - 4}$, on the domain $\mathbb{R} - \{4\}$.

questions.stem: In the simplest form: $n(x) = \dfrac{2x + 8}{x^2 + 5x + 4} + \dfrac{2}{x + 1} = \dots$
solution: Factorize the first fraction: $\dfrac{2(x + 4)}{(x + 1)(x + 4)}$; the domain of $n$ is $\mathbb{R} - \{-4, -1\}$.
Reduce it: $\dfrac{2}{x + 1}$.

learning_objectives.label: Multiplying and dividing algebraic fractions
learning_objectives.description: Multiply and divide algebraic fractions; multiplicative inverse; the domain of a quotient excludes the zeroes of both denominators and of the divisor's numerator.

questions.stem: The multiplicative inverse of the algebraic fraction $n(x) = \dfrac{x - 3}{x + 7}$ is $\dots$
solution: The multiplicative inverse $n^{-1}(x)$ is the reciprocal of the fraction.
Check: $n(x) \times n^{-1}(x) = \dfrac{x - 3}{x + 7} \times \dfrac{x + 7}{x - 3} = 1$ on the common domain $\mathbb{R} - \{-7, 3\}$.

questions.stem: In the simplest form: $\dfrac{x^2 - 1}{x} \times \dfrac{x^2}{x + 1} = \dots$
solution: Factorize: $\dfrac{(x - 1)(x + 1)}{x} \times \dfrac{x^2}{x + 1}$, on the common domain $\mathbb{R} - \{-1, 0\}$.
Cancel $(x + 1)$ and one factor $x$: $(x - 1) \times x$.
So the product $= x(x - 1) = x^2 - x$.

questions.stem: In the simplest form: $\dfrac{x - 2}{x + 1} \div \dfrac{x - 2}{x + 5} = \dots$
solution: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its multiplicative inverse: $\dfrac{x - 2}{x + 1} \times \dfrac{x + 5}{x - 2}$.
The domain excludes the zeroes of $(x + 1)$, $(x + 5)$ and of the divisor's numerator $(x - 2)$: $\mathbb{R} - \{-5, -1, 2\}$.
Cancel $(x - 2)$: the quotient $= \dfrac{x + 5}{x + 1}$.

questions.stem: The domain of $n(x) = \dfrac{x}{x - 1} \div \dfrac{x - 3}{x + 2}$ is $\dots$
solution: For $n_1 \div n_2$ the domain is $\mathbb{R} - (Z(f_2) \cup Z(f_3) \cup Z(f_4))$: the zeroes of both denominators and of the divisor's numerator.
$Z(x - 1) = \{1\}$, $Z(x + 2) = \{-2\}$, and the divisor's numerator gives $Z(x - 3) = \{3\}$.
Therefore the domain is $\mathbb{R} - \{-2, 1, 3\}$.

questions.stem: If $n(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{2x^2 + 6x} \div \dfrac{x - 3}{4x}$, find $n(5)$.
solution: Factorize: $n(x) = \dfrac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{2x(x + 3)} \div \dfrac{x - 3}{4x}$, with domain $\mathbb{R} - \{-3, 0, 3\}$.
Multiply by the inverse: $\dfrac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{2x(x + 3)} \times \dfrac{4x}{x - 3}$.
Cancel $(x - 3)$, $(x + 3)$ and $x$: $n(x) = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2$ for every $x$ in the domain.

learning_objectives.label: Probability of an event: P(A) = n(A)/n(S)
learning_objectives.description: Write the sample space S of a random experiment; for an event A ⊂ S compute P(A) = n(A)/n(S); recognize the impossible event (P = 0), the certain event (P = 1), and place probabilities on the scale from 0 to 1 written as fractions or percentages.

questions.stem: A regular die is rolled once and the upper face is observed. The probability of getting a number less than 7 equals …
solution: Write the sample space: $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, so $n(S) = 6$.
The event of getting a number less than 7 is $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\} = S$ itself, so its number of elements $= 6$.
$P(\text{number} < 7) = \dfrac{6}{6} = 1$ — every face of the die is less than 7, so it is a certain event and its probability is $1$.

questions.stem: A regular die is rolled once. The probability of getting the number 8 equals …
solution: The sample space is $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ and $n(S) = 6$.
The event of getting 8 has no elements in $S$ (the die has no face 8), so it is the impossible event: its set is $\phi$ and $n(\phi) = 0$.
$P(\text{getting } 8) = \dfrac{0}{6} = 0$.

questions.stem: A box contains 6 white balls and 4 red balls. If a ball is drawn randomly, calculate the probability that the drawn ball is red.
solution: The box contains $6 + 4 = 10$ identical balls, all equally likely to be drawn, so $n(S) = 10$.
The event of drawing a red ball has $n(A) = 4$ elements.
$P(\text{red}) = \dfrac{n(A)}{n(S)} = \dfrac{4}{10} = \dfrac{2}{5} = 0.4$.

questions.stem: A spinner is divided into 10 equal sectors: 4 green, 3 yellow, 2 blue and 1 red. The probability that the indicator stops on a yellow sector equals …
solution: The 10 sectors are equal, so all outcomes are equally likely and $n(S) = 10$.
The yellow sectors are $3$, so $n(\text{yellow}) = 3$.
$P(\text{yellow}) = \dfrac{n(\text{yellow})}{n(S)} = \dfrac{3}{10}$.

questions.stem: A set of identical cards numbered from 1 to 8 is mixed well and a card is drawn randomly. The probability that the drawn card has a prime number equals …
solution: The sample space is $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8\}$, so $n(S) = 8$.
The event of drawing a prime number is $B = \{2, 3, 5, 7\}$, so $n(B) = 4$ (remember: 1 is not prime).
$P(B) = \dfrac{n(B)}{n(S)} = \dfrac{4}{8} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.stem: If the probability of an event is $P(A) = \dfrac{3}{4}$, write $P(A)$ as a percentage. (Answer in %.)
solution: Probability can be written as a fraction or as a percentage.
So $P(A) = 75\%$ — on the probability scale this is 'more likely' (between $\frac{1}{2}$ and the certain event 1).

questions.stem: Which of the following values CANNOT be the probability of an event?
solution: For any event $A \subset S$: $0 \le n(A) \le n(S)$, so $P(A) = \dfrac{n(A)}{n(S)}$ is always between 0 and 1.
$P = 0$ is the impossible event and $P = 1$ is the certain event; $0.25 = \frac{1}{4}$ lies between them on the scale.
$1.2 > 1$, so it cannot be the probability of any event.

questions.stem: Identical cards numbered from 1 to 12 are mixed well and one card is drawn randomly. Find the probability that the drawn card has a number divisible by 4.
solution: The sample space is $S = \{1, 2, 3, \dots, 12\}$, so $n(S) = 12$.
The event of a number divisible by 4 is $A = \{4, 8, 12\}$, so $n(A) = 3$.

learning_objectives.label: Intersection of two events and mutually exclusive events
learning_objectives.description: For events A, B of a sample space S, form A ∩ B — the event that A and B occur together — using Venn diagrams; compute P(A ∩ B) = n(A ∩ B)/n(S); recognize mutually exclusive events, where A ∩ B = φ and P(A ∩ B) = 0.

questions.stem: If A and B are two events from a sample space S, then $A \cap B$ means …
solution: Events are subsets of the sample space S, so operations on events are like operations on sets.
The intersection $A \cap B$ means the events A and B occur together — the outcome of the experiment belongs to both sets.
The occurrence of at least one event is the union $A \cup B$, and the occurrence of A only is the difference $A - B$.

questions.stem: It is said that A and B are two mutually exclusive events if …
solution: A and B are mutually exclusive events if $A \cap B = \phi$: the two events cannot occur at the same time.
In the Venn diagram they appear as two separate (distant) sets, and $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{0}{n(S)} = 0$.

questions.stem: Identical cards numbered from 1 to 10 are mixed well and a card is drawn randomly. Event A: the card has an even number; event B: the card has a prime number. The probability that A and B occur together equals …
solution: Occurring together means $A \cap B = \{2\}$ — the only even prime — so $n(A \cap B) = 1$.
$P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{n(A \cap B)}{n(S)} = \dfrac{1}{10}$.

questions.stem: A regular die is rolled once. Event A: getting an even number; event B: getting a number greater than 3. Find $n(A \cap B)$, the number of elements of the event that A and B occur together.
solution: $A \cap B = \{4, 6\}$ — the outcomes that are even AND greater than 3.
So $n(A \cap B) = 2$ (and $P(A \cap B) = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$).

questions.stem: A regular die is rolled once. Event A: getting an even number; event B: getting an odd number. The probability of the occurrence of A and B together equals …
solution: A number cannot be even and odd at the same time, so $A \cap B = \phi$ and $n(A \cap B) = 0$: A and B are mutually exclusive events.
$P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{0}{6} = 0$.

questions.stem: Identical cards numbered from 1 to 12 are mixed well and a card is drawn randomly. Event A: the number is divisible by 3; event B: the number is divisible by 4. Then $P(A \cap B)$ equals …
solution: $A \cap B = \{12\}$ — the only number from 1 to 12 divisible by both 3 and 4 — so $n(A \cap B) = 1$.
$P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{1}{12}$.

questions.stem: A regular die is rolled once. Which pair of events is MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE?
solution: Two events are mutually exclusive when their intersection is $\phi$ — they cannot occur at the same time.
Even $\{2,4,6\}$ and odd $\{1,3,5\}$: intersection $= \phi$ ✓ mutually exclusive.

Even $\{2,4,6\}$ and prime $\{2,3,5\}$ share $\{2\}$; odd $\{1,3,5\}$ and prime $\{2,3,5\}$ share $\{3,5\}$; greater than 2 $\{3,4,5,6\}$ and less than 5 $\{1,2,3,4\}$ share $\{3,4\}$ — none of these are mutually exclusive.

questions.stem: A and B are two events of a sample space S of a random experiment where $n(S) = 20$ and $n(A \cap B) = 5$. Find the probability of the occurrence of the two events together.
solution: The probability of the occurrence of A and B together is $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{n(A \cap B)}{n(S)}$.
Substitute: $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{5}{20} = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$.

learning_objectives.label: Union of two events and the addition rule
learning_objectives.description: Form A ∪ B — the occurrence of A or B or both (at least one event) — and compute its probability by counting or by the rule P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B); for mutually exclusive events P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).

questions.stem: If A and B are two events from a sample space S, then $A \cup B$ means the occurrence of …
solution: The union $A \cup B$ means the occurrence of the two events A or B or both.
In other words: the occurrence of at least one of the two events.
The occurrence of the two events together is the intersection $A \cap B$.

questions.stem: For any two events A and B of a sample space S, $P(A \cup B)$ equals …
solution: Adding $P(A) + P(B)$ counts the elements of $A \cap B$ twice, so we subtract them once.
$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.
Only when A and B are mutually exclusive ($A \cap B = \phi$, $P(A \cap B) = 0$) does this become $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.

questions.stem: A and B are two events in the sample space of a random experiment where $P(A) = 0.3$, $P(B) = 0.4$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$. Find $P(A \cup B)$.
solution: $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$.
Substitute: $P(A \cup B) = 0.3 + 0.4 - 0.2$.

questions.stem: A and B are two MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE events where $P(A) = 0.35$ and $P(B) = 0.25$. Find $P(A \cup B)$.
solution: A and B are mutually exclusive, so $A \cap B = \phi$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0$.
$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B)$.

questions.stem: Identical cards numbered from 1 to 10 are mixed well and a card is drawn randomly. Event A: the number is even; event B: the number is divisible by 3. The probability of the occurrence of A or B equals …
solution: Occurrence of A or B means $A \cup B = \{2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10\}$, so $n(A \cup B) = 7$.
$P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{n(A \cup B)}{n(S)} = \dfrac{7}{10}$.
Check by the rule: $P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{5}{10} + \dfrac{3}{10} - \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{7}{10}$ ✓ (since $A \cap B = \{6\}$).

questions.stem: A and B are two events in the sample space of a random experiment where $P(A) = 0.5$, $P(B) = 0.6$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.8$. Find $P(A \cap B)$.
solution: From the rule $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)$, we get $P(A \cap B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cup B)$.
Substitute: $P(A \cap B) = 0.5 + 0.6 - 0.8$.

questions.stem: A regular die is rolled once. Event A: getting a number less than 3; event B: getting a prime number. Then $P(A \cup B)$ equals …
solution: $A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 5\}$, so $n(A \cup B) = 4$ and $P(A \cup B) = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.
Check by the rule: $A \cap B = \{2\}$, so $P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{2}{6} + \dfrac{3}{6} - \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$ ✓.

questions.stem: A and B are two mutually exclusive events in the sample space of a random experiment where $P(B) = 0.3$ and $P(A \cup B) = 0.85$. Find $P(A)$.
solution: A and B are mutually exclusive, so $P(A \cap B) = 0$ and $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.

learning_objectives.label: The complementary event
learning_objectives.description: For A ⊂ S, the complementary event A′ satisfies A ∪ A′ = S and A ∩ A′ = φ (the event and its complement are mutually exclusive); use P(A) + P(A′) = 1, i.e. P(A′) = 1 − P(A).

questions.stem: If $A \subset S$, then the complementary event $A'$ to the event A satisfies …
solution: The complementary event $A'$ contains all the elements of the sample space S that are not in A.
So $A \cup A' = S$ and $A \cap A' = \phi$ — the event and the complementary event are two mutually exclusive events.
It follows that $P(A) + P(A') = P(S) = 1$.

questions.stem: A is an event of the sample space of a random experiment and $A'$ is its complementary event. If $P(A) = 0.7$, find $P(A')$.
solution: Substitute: $P(A') = 1 - 0.7$.

questions.stem: A box has identical balls numbered from 1 to 9 and one ball is drawn randomly. Event A: getting a number divisible by 3. The probability of the complementary event $A'$ equals …
solution: $A'$ is the event of NOT getting a number divisible by 3: $A' = \{1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8\}$, $n(A') = 6$, so $P(A') = \dfrac{6}{9} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.
Another solution: $P(A') = 1 - P(A) = 1 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

questions.stem: A spinner is divided into 10 equal sectors, 3 of them are red. Find the probability that the indicator does NOT stop on a red sector.
solution: The 10 sectors are equal, so $n(S) = 10$; the event R (red) has $n(R) = 3$, so $P(R) = \dfrac{3}{10}$.
Not stopping on red is the complementary event $R'$.

questions.stem: A is an event of a sample space S and $A'$ is its complementary event. If $P(A') = \dfrac{2}{5}$, then $P(A)$ equals …
A is an event of the sample space of a random experiment and $A'$ is its complementary event. If $P(A) = 3\,P(A')$, find $P(A')$.
solution: Substitute: $3\,P(A') + P(A') = 1$, so $4\,P(A') = 1$.

questions.stem: The event A and its complementary event $A'$ are always …
solution: By definition $A \cap A' = \phi$, so the event and the complementary event are two mutually exclusive events — they can never occur together.
Also $A \cup A' = S$: one of them must occur, and $P(A) + P(A') = P(S) = 1$.
Their probabilities are equal only in the special case $P(A) = P(A') = \frac{1}{2}$, not always.

questions.stem: A class contains 30 students, 12 of them wear glasses. If a student is selected randomly, find the probability that the selected student does NOT wear glasses.
solution: $n(S) = 30$; let A be the event that the selected student wears glasses, $n(A) = 12$, so $P(A) = \dfrac{12}{30} = \dfrac{2}{5}$.
Not wearing glasses is the complementary event $A'$, with $n(A') = 30 - 12 = 18$.
$P(A') = \dfrac{18}{30} = \dfrac{3}{5} = 0.6$; another solution: $P(A') = 1 - P(A) = 1 - \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{3}{5}$.

learning_objectives.label: The difference between two events
learning_objectives.description: A − B is the event that A occurs and B does not occur (the occurrence of A only); note that (A − B) ∪ (A ∩ B) = A; apply it with Venn diagrams to 'only one' and 'exactly one' problems.

questions.stem: If A and B are two events of a sample space S, then $A - B$ is the event of …
solution: $A - B$ (read: A difference B) is the event of the occurrence of A and the non-occurrence of B.
That is: the occurrence of the event A only.
The occurrence together is $A \cap B$, and at least one is $A \cup B$.

questions.stem: For any two events A and B of a sample space S: $(A - B) \cup (A \cap B) = $ …
solution: $A - B$ is the part of A outside B, and $A \cap B$ is the part of A inside B.
Together these two parts make up all of A: $(A - B) \cup (A \cap B) = A$.
In the Venn diagram, the set A is split into exactly these two regions.

questions.stem: A class contains 50 students: 22 play football, 18 play basketball and 10 play both games. If a student is selected randomly, find the probability that the student plays football ONLY.
solution: Let A = plays football and B = plays basketball: $n(S) = 50$, $n(A) = 22$, $n(B) = 18$, $n(A \cap B) = 10$.
Playing football only is the difference $A - B$: $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B) = 22 - 10 = 12$.

questions.stem: In the same class of 50 students (22 play football, 18 play basketball, 10 play both), the probability that a randomly selected student plays basketball ONLY equals …
solution: Playing basketball only is the difference $B - A$: the student plays basketball and does not play football.

questions.stem: In the same class of 50 students (22 play football, 18 play basketball, 10 play both), find the probability that a randomly selected student plays NEITHER of the two games.
solution: Split the class in the Venn diagram: football only $= 22 - 10 = 12$, both $= 10$, basketball only $= 18 - 10 = 8$.
Students playing at least one game: $n(A \cup B) = 12 + 10 + 8 = 30$.
Playing neither game is the complementary event of $A \cup B$: $n = 50 - 30 = 20$.
$P(\text{neither}) = \dfrac{20}{50} = \dfrac{2}{5} = 0.4$.

questions.stem: In the same class of 50 students (22 play football, 18 play basketball, 10 play both), the probability that a randomly selected student plays EXACTLY ONE of the two games equals …
solution: Exactly one game means: football only OR basketball only — the union $(A - B) \cup (B - A)$ of two mutually exclusive events.
$n(A - B) = 22 - 10 = 12$ and $n(B - A) = 18 - 10 = 8$, so together $12 + 8 = 20$ students.

questions.stem: Identical cards numbered from 1 to 10 are mixed well and a card is drawn randomly. Event A: the number is even; event B: the number is divisible by 4. Then $P(A - B)$ equals …
solution: $A - B$ is the event that A occurs and B does not: $A - B = \{2, 6, 10\}$, so $n(A - B) = 3$.

questions.stem: A and B are two events of a sample space S where $n(S) = 30$, $n(A) = 15$ and $n(A \cap B) = 6$. Find $P(A - B)$.
solution: Since $(A - B) \cup (A \cap B) = A$ and the two parts are mutually exclusive: $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)$.

learning_objectives.label: Ordered pairs and their equality
learning_objectives.description: Identify ordered pairs, first/second projections; apply (a,b)=(x,y) ⟺ a=x and b=y.

solution: Two ordered pairs are equal when their corresponding projections are equal: $(a,b)=(x,y) \Rightarrow a=x,\ b=y$.
So $a = 3$ and $b = 5$.
Therefore $a + b = 3 + 5 = 8$.

questions.stem: If $(x - 4,\ 7) = (9,\ y + 2)$, find the value of $x \times y$.
solution: Equate first projections: $x - 4 = 9$, so $x = 13$.
Equate second projections: $7 = y + 2$, so $y = 5$.
Therefore $x \times y = 13 \times 5 = 65$.

questions.stem: If $(a - 2,\ b + 1) = (b - 4,\ 3)$, then the ordered pair $(a, b) =$ ?
solution: From the second projections: $b + 1 = 3$, so $b = 2$.
From the first projections: $a - 2 = b - 4 = 2 - 4 = -2$, so $a = 0$.
Therefore $(a, b) = (0, 2)$.

learning_objectives.label: Cartesian product of finite sets
learning_objectives.description: Form X×Y for finite non-empty sets; use n(X×Y)=n(X)×n(Y); recognize X×Y ≠ Y×X and X².

questions.stem: If $X = \{1, 2\}$ and $Y = \{5\}$, then $X \times Y =$ ?
solution: $X \times Y$ is the set of ordered pairs whose first projection is in $X$ and second projection is in $Y$.
Pair each element of $X$ with each element of $Y$: $(1,5)$ and $(2,5)$.

questions.stem: If $n(X) = 3$ and $n(Y) = 4$, find $n(X \times Y)$.
solution: For finite non-empty sets, $n(X \times Y) = n(X) \times n(Y)$.
$n(X \times Y) = 3 \times 4 = 12$.

questions.stem: If $n(X \times Y) = 15$ and $n(X) = 3$, find $n(Y^2)$.
solution: $n(X \times Y) = n(X) \times n(Y)$, so $15 = 3 \times n(Y)$, giving $n(Y) = 5$.
$Y^2 = Y \times Y$, so $n(Y^2) = n(Y) \times n(Y) = 5 \times 5 = 25$.

learning_objectives.label: Representing Cartesian products
learning_objectives.description: Represent X×Y by arrow diagrams and Cartesian (graphical net) diagrams.

questions.stem: In the arrow diagram of $X \times Y$, each arrow starts from…
solution: The arrow diagram represents each ordered pair by an arrow from its first projection to its second projection.
First projections are the elements of $X$, so every arrow starts from an element of $X$.

questions.stem: If $X = \{a, b\}$ and $Y = \{1, 2, 3\}$, how many arrows are in the arrow diagram of $X \times Y$?
solution: Each ordered pair in $X \times Y$ is represented by one arrow.
$n(X \times Y) = n(X) \times n(Y) = 2 \times 3 = 6$.
So the diagram has 6 arrows.

learning_objectives.label: Cartesian products of infinite sets; the coordinate plane
learning_objectives.description: Represent N×N, Z×Z, Q×Q, R×R; identify quadrants and axes.

questions.stem: The point $(-2, 5)$ is located in the…
solution: In the second quadrant, $x < 0$ and $y > 0$.
Here $x = -2 < 0$ and $y = 5 > 0$, so the point lies in the second quadrant.

questions.stem: The point $(0, -3)$ is located…
solution: A point with first coordinate $0$ lies on the y-axis.
$(0, -3)$ has $x = 0$, so it lies on the y-axis (below the origin).

learning_objectives.label: Relations between sets
learning_objectives.description: Define a relation from X to Y as a subset of X×Y; write and represent relations.

questions.stem: If $R$ is a relation from $X$ to $Y$, then $R$ is a subset of…
solution: A relation from $X$ to $Y$ connects elements of $X$ with elements of $Y$ using ordered pairs $(a, b)$ with $a \in X$, $b \in Y$.
All such pairs belong to $X \times Y$, so $R \subseteq X \times Y$.

questions.stem: If $X = \{1, 2\}$, $Y = \{2, 4, 6\}$ and $R$ is a relation from $X$ to $Y$ where $a\,R\,b$ means $b = 2a$, then $R =$ ?
solution: Test each $a \in X$: for $a = 1$, $b = 2(1) = 2 \in Y$ ✓; for $a = 2$, $b = 2(2) = 4 \in Y$ ✓.
So $R = \{(1,2), (2,4)\}$. Note $(3,6)$ is impossible since $3 \notin X$.

questions.stem: If $n(X) = 2$ and $n(Y) = 3$, how many different relations can be defined from $X$ to $Y$? (Hint: every subset of $X \times Y$ is a relation.)
solution: $n(X \times Y) = 2 \times 3 = 6$.
Every subset of $X \times Y$ is a relation from $X$ to $Y$, and a set with 6 elements has $2^6$ subsets.
$2^6 = 64$ relations.

learning_objectives.label: Relation on a set
learning_objectives.description: Identify and represent relations from a set to itself (R ⊆ X×X).

questions.stem: If $X = \{-1, 0, 1\}$ and $R$ is a relation on $X$ where $a\,R\,b$ means $a + b = 0$, then $R =$ ?
solution: A relation on $X$ pairs elements of $X$ with elements of $X$.

learning_objectives.label: The function concept
learning_objectives.description: Determine whether a relation is a function: each element of X appears exactly once as a first projection; use f: X→Y notation.

questions.stem: A relation from $X$ to $Y$ is a function if…
solution: By definition (Lesson 1-3): a relation from $X$ to $Y$ is a function if each element of $X$ appears only once as a first projection in the ordered pairs.
Elements of $Y$ may repeat or be unused — the condition is only on $X$.

questions.stem: If $X = \{1, 2, 3\}$, which of the following relations on $X$ is a function on $X$?
solution: A function on $X$ needs every element of $X$ to appear exactly once as a first projection.
Option B: 1 appears twice as a first projection ✗. Options C and D: the element 3 (resp. 1) never appears as a first projection ✗.
Option A: 1, 2, 3 each appear exactly once as first projections ✓.

questions.stem: $X = \{2, 3, 4\}$, $Y = \{y : y \in \mathbb{N},\ 2 \le y < 9\}$, and $R$ from $X$ to $Y$ where $a\,R\,b$ means $a = \frac{1}{2}b$. Is $R$ a function from $X$ to $Y$, and what is $R$?
solution: $a = \frac{1}{2}b$ means $b = 2a$: for $a=2, b=4$; $a=3, b=6$; $a=4, b=8$ — all in $Y$.
Every element of $X$ appears exactly once as a first projection, so $R$ is a function: $R = \{(2,4), (3,6), (4,8)\}$.

learning_objectives.label: Domain, codomain and range
learning_objectives.description: Identify the domain, codomain and range of a function; range ⊆ codomain.

solution: The range is the set of images of the elements of the domain — the second projections actually used.
Range $= \{3, 5, 7\}$; note it is a subset of the codomain $Y$, and $2 \in Y$ is not an image.

questions.stem: For $f : X \to Y$ where $X = \{2, 3, 4\}$ and $f(x) = 2x$, which statement is correct?
solution: The domain is $X = \{2,3,4\}$; the images are $f(2)=4$, $f(3)=6$, $f(4)=8$.
The range $\{4,6,8\}$ is the set of images, and the range is always a subset of the codomain $Y$.
The codomain may be larger than the range, so C is wrong.

learning_objectives.label: Polynomial functions and evaluation
learning_objectives.description: Identify polynomial functions and their degree; evaluate f(x) at given values.

questions.stem: Which of the following represents a polynomial function?
solution: A polynomial has the form $f(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + \dots + a_n x^n$ with natural-number powers of $x$ only.
$\frac{1}{x} = x^{-1}$ and $\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}$ are not natural powers, so B, C, D are excluded.
$f(x) = x^3 + x^2 + 3$ is a polynomial (degree 3).
Substitute $x = -2$ into the rule of the function.

questions.stem: If $f(x) = x^2 - 3x$ and $g(x) = x - 3$, find the value of $f(3) + g(3)$.
The degree of the polynomial function $f(x) = x(x - 2x^2)$ is…
solution: Expand: $f(x) = x \cdot x - x \cdot 2x^2 = x^2 - 2x^3$.
The degree is the highest power of $x$, which is 3.

learning_objectives.label: Linear and constant functions
learning_objectives.description: Graph f(x)=ax+b; special cases f(x)=ax through the origin and constant f(x)=b parallel to x-axis.

questions.stem: The graph of $f(x) = ax$ where $a \neq 0$ is a straight line that passes through…
solution: $f(0) = a \times 0 = 0$, so the point $(0, 0)$ always lies on the graph.
The graph of $f(x) = ax$, $a \neq 0$, is a straight line through the origin (Remark 2, Lesson 1-4).

questions.stem: Which point lies on the graph of the linear function $f(x) = 2x - 3$?
solution: A point $(x, y)$ lies on the graph when $y = f(x)$.
Test A: $f(2) = 2(2) - 3 = 1$ ✓, so $(2, 1)$ lies on the graph.

questions.stem: The graph of the constant function $f(x) = 5$ is a straight line…
solution: For every $x$, $f(x) = 5$: all points have the form $(x, 5)$.
These points form a horizontal line at height 5, parallel to the x-axis (special case, Lesson 1-4).

learning_objectives.label: Quadratic functions
learning_objectives.description: Graph f(x)=ax²+bx+c; vertex (−b/2a, f(−b/2a)), axis of symmetry, opening direction, max/min value.

questions.stem: The minimum value of the quadratic function $f(x) = x^2$ is…
solution: $f(x) = x^2$ has $a = 1 > 0$, so the curve opens upward and has a minimum at its vertex.
The vertex is at $x = \frac{-b}{2a} = 0$, and $f(0) = 0$.
The minimum value is $0$.

questions.stem: Find the x-coordinate of the vertex of the curve of $f(x) = 2x^2 - 8x + 3$.
solution: For $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$, the vertex has x-coordinate $\frac{-b}{2a}$.

questions.stem: The function $f(x) = -x^2 + 4x - 1$ has a…
solution: $a = -1 < 0$, so the curve opens downward and the function has a maximum value (property 3, Lesson 1-4).
Vertex x-coordinate: $\frac{-b}{2a} = \frac{-4}{-2} = 2$.

learning_objectives.label: Ratio and its properties
learning_objectives.description: Write the ratio between two quantities as a : b or a/b, name the antecedent and consequent, and apply the properties: multiplying both terms by a nonzero constant keeps the ratio, while adding a number to both terms changes it (and a/b = 3/5 does not force a = 3, b = 5).

questions.stem: In the ratio $4 : 9$, the antecedent is …
solution: The ratio between two numbers $a$ and $b$ is written $a : b$ or $\frac{a}{b}$: $a$ is called the antecedent and $b$ is called the consequent.
In $4 : 9$ the first term is 4, so the antecedent is 4 (and 9 is the consequent); together they are the two terms of the ratio.

questions.stem: In a class there are 6 boys and 8 girls. The ratio between the number of boys and the number of girls in its simplest form is …
solution: The ratio between the number of boys and the number of girls is $6 : 8$.
Dividing both terms by the same nonzero number does not change the ratio: divide by 2.
$6 : 8 = 3 : 4$ in simplest form.

questions.stem: Which of the following ratios is equal to the ratio $3 : 5$?
solution: A ratio is not changed if each of its two terms is multiplied by the same fixed nonzero amount.
Multiply both terms of $3 : 5$ by 4: $3 \times 4 = 12$ and $5 \times 4 = 20$, so $3 : 5 = 12 : 20$.
$5 : 7$ comes from adding 2 to each term (which changes the ratio), $9 : 25$ squares the terms, and $5 : 3$ reverses the order.

questions.stem: If $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{2}{7}$, then which of the following is certainly true?
solution: $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{2}{7}$ does NOT force $a = 2$ and $b = 7$: for example $a = 4$, $b = 14$ gives the same ratio (just as $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{3}{5}$ does not mean $a = 3$, $b = 5$).
It only means the two numbers are in the ratio $2 : 7$, i.e. $a = 2m$ and $b = 7m$ for some nonzero constant $m$.
Then $a + b = 9m$, which equals 9 only when $m = 1$.

questions.stem: When 3 is added to each of the two terms of the ratio $2 : 3$, the resulting ratio in its simplest form is $a : b$. Find $a + b$.
solution: Adding 3 to each term: $(2 + 3) : (3 + 3) = 5 : 6$.
$5 : 6$ is already in simplest form, so $a = 5$ and $b = 6$ — note the ratio changed ($\frac{2}{3} \neq \frac{5}{6}$), because adding a number to both terms changes a ratio.

learning_objectives.label: Ratio equations
learning_objectives.description: Find an unknown number which, when added to (or subtracted from) the two terms of a given ratio — possibly as its square — produces a required ratio, by cross-multiplying and solving.

questions.stem: If the same nonzero number is added to both terms of the ratio $3 : 5$, then in general the ratio …
solution: Test with a number, say add 5: $\frac{3+5}{5+5} = \frac{8}{10} = \frac{4}{5} \neq \frac{3}{5}$.
So adding the same number to both terms changes the ratio in general — unlike multiplying both terms by a nonzero constant, which keeps it.
(The ratio only approaches $1 : 1$ as the added number grows very large; it does not equal it.)

questions.stem: Find the number which, if added to the two terms of the ratio $5 : 9$, makes it $3 : 4$.
solution: Consider the number is $x$: $\frac{x + 5}{x + 9} = \frac{3}{4}$.
Cross-multiply: $4(x + 5) = 3(x + 9)$, so $4x + 20 = 3x + 27$.

questions.stem: The number which, if added to the two terms of the ratio $3 : 8$, makes it $2 : 3$ is …
solution: Consider the number is $x$: $\frac{x + 3}{x + 8} = \frac{2}{3}$.
Cross-multiply: $3(x + 3) = 2(x + 8)$, so $3x + 9 = 2x + 16$.

questions.stem: Find the positive number which, if we add its square to each of the two terms of the ratio $1 : 11$, the ratio becomes $1 : 2$.
solution: Consider the number is $x$, so we add $x^2$ to each term: $\frac{x^2 + 1}{x^2 + 11} = \frac{1}{2}$.
$x^2 = 9$, and since the number is positive, $x = 3$.

questions.stem: Find the number which, if subtracted from the two terms of the ratio $9 : 13$, makes it $1 : 2$.
solution: Consider the number is $x$: $\frac{9 - x}{13 - x} = \frac{1}{2}$.
Cross-multiply: $2(9 - x) = 13 - x$, so $18 - 2x = 13 - x$.

learning_objectives.label: Proportion, its terms, and the fourth proportional
learning_objectives.description: Define a proportion as the equality of two or more ratios a/b = c/d; name the first–fourth proportionals, extremes and means; use 'product of the extremes = product of the means' (ad = bc) to test proportionality and find a fourth proportional.

questions.stem: The proportion is …
solution: By definition (Lesson 2-2): the proportion is the equality of two ratios or more.
For example, $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$ means $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ are in proportion.

questions.stem: In the proportion $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$, the extremes are …
solution: In $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$: $a$ is the first proportional, $b$ the second, $c$ the third and $d$ the fourth.
$a$ and $d$ (the first and last terms) are called the extremes, while $b$ and $c$ are called the means.

questions.stem: Find the fourth proportional for the numbers $3,\ 9,\ 5$.
solution: Consider the fourth proportional to be $x$: $\frac{3}{9} = \frac{5}{x}$.
Product of the extremes = product of the means: $3x = 9 \times 5 = 45$.
$x = \frac{45}{3} = 15$, so the fourth proportional is 15.

questions.stem: If $\frac{2}{x} = \frac{6}{21}$, find the value of $x$.
solution: The two ratios are equal, so the four numbers $2, x, 6, 21$ are in proportion.
Product of the extremes = product of the means: $2 \times 21 = 6x$.

questions.stem: Which of the following groups of numbers (in this order) are in proportion?
solution: Four numbers $a, b, c, d$ are in proportion when $ad = bc$ (product of the extremes = product of the means).
Check C: $2 \times 15 = 30$ and $6 \times 5 = 30$ ✓, so $\frac{2}{6} = \frac{5}{15}$.

Check the others: A: $3 	imes 6 = 18 
eq 4 	imes 5 = 20$; B: $1 	imes 5 = 5 
eq 2 	imes 3 = 6$; D: $2 	imes 5 = 10 
eq 3 	imes 4 = 12$.

questions.stem: Find the number that, if added to each of the numbers $2,\ 4,\ 7,\ 11$, makes them proportional.
solution: Consider the number is $x$, i.e. $2+x,\ 4+x,\ 7+x,\ 11+x$ are in proportion: $\frac{2+x}{4+x} = \frac{7+x}{11+x}$.
Product of the extremes = product of the means: $(2+x)(11+x) = (4+x)(7+x)$.

learning_objectives.label: Properties of proportion
learning_objectives.description: Use the properties of a/b = c/d — a = mc and b = md, a/c = b/d, and the sum property (a m₁ + c m₂)/(b m₁ + d m₂) = one of the ratios — to evaluate ratio expressions by substituting a = km, b = lm.

questions.stem: If $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$, then …
solution: This is property 2 of proportion: the product of the extremes equals the product of the means.
The extremes are $a$ and $d$, and the means are $b$ and $c$, so $ad = bc$.
For example $\frac{4}{2} = \frac{16}{8}$ gives $4 \times 8 = 2 \times 16 = 32$.

questions.stem: If $\frac{x}{y} = \frac{3}{4}$, find the value of the ratio $\frac{2x + 3y}{6y - 2x}$.
solution: Consider $x = 3m$, $y = 4m$ where $m$ is a nonzero constant.
Denominator: $6y - 2x = 6(4m) - 2(3m) = 24m - 6m = 18m$.

questions.stem: If $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{2}{3}$, find the value of $(5a + 2b) : (4a - 2b)$.
solution: Consider $a = 2m$, $b = 3m$ where $m$ is a nonzero constant.

questions.stem: If $\frac{a}{2} = \frac{b}{5} = \frac{c}{7}$, find the value of $\frac{a + b + c}{c}$.
solution: Let $\frac{a}{2} = \frac{b}{5} = \frac{c}{7} = m$ (a nonzero constant), so $a = 2m$, $b = 5m$, $c = 7m$.
This uses the sum property: the sum of antecedents over the sum of consequents equals one of the ratios.
$\frac{a + b + c}{c} = \frac{2m + 5m + 7m}{7m} = \frac{14m}{7m} = 2$.

questions.stem: If $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$, then $\frac{a + b}{b} = $ …
solution: Consider $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d} = m$, so $a = bm$ and $c = dm$.
$\frac{a + b}{b} = \frac{bm + b}{b} = m + 1$.
$\frac{c + d}{d} = \frac{dm + d}{d} = m + 1$ as well, so $\frac{a + b}{b} = \frac{c + d}{d}$.

learning_objectives.label: Continued proportion and the middle proportional
learning_objectives.description: Recognize a, b, c in continued proportion when a/b = b/c, so b² = ac and the middle proportional b = ±√(ac); find middle and third proportionals.

questions.stem: The quantities $a$, $b$ and $c$ are in continued proportion if …
solution: By definition: $a$, $b$, $c$ are in continued proportion if $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{b}{c}$.
Then $a$ is the first proportional, $b$ the middle proportional, and $c$ the third proportional.
Cross-multiplying gives the key relation $b^2 = ac$.

questions.stem: Find the positive middle proportional between $4$ and $25$.
solution: If $b$ is the middle proportional between $a$ and $c$, then $b^2 = ac$, so $b = \pm\sqrt{ac}$.
$b = \pm\sqrt{4 \times 25} = \pm\sqrt{100} = \pm 10$.
The positive middle proportional is $10$.

questions.stem: The middle proportional between $2$ and $32$ equals …
solution: The middle proportional $b$ satisfies $b^2 = ac$, so $b = \pm\sqrt{ac}$.
$b = \pm\sqrt{2 \times 32} = \pm\sqrt{64} = \pm 8$.
Both $8$ and $-8$ work (check: $\frac{2}{-8} = \frac{-8}{32} = -\frac{1}{4}$), so the answer is $\pm 8$, not $8$ only.

questions.stem: If $4,\ 6,\ x$ are in continued proportion, find the value of $x$ (the third proportional).
solution: $4, 6, x$ in continued proportion means $\frac{4}{6} = \frac{6}{x}$.
Cross-multiply: $4x = 36$ (this is $b^2 = ac$ with $b = 6$).

questions.stem: If $a,\ 6,\ 12$ are in continued proportion, find the value of $a$.
solution: $a, 6, 12$ in continued proportion means $\frac{a}{6} = \frac{6}{12}$.

questions.stem: $a,\ b,\ c$ are in continued proportion where $a = 4$, $c = 16$ and $b > 0$. Find the value of $\frac{a + b}{b + c}$.
solution: $b$ is the middle proportional: $b^2 = ac = 4 \times 16 = 64$, and since $b > 0$, $b = 8$.
$\frac{a + b}{b + c} = \frac{12}{24} = 0.5$ — which is exactly the common ratio $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{4}{8}$.

learning_objectives.label: Direct variation
learning_objectives.description: Express y ∝ x as y = mx (m constant ≠ 0), use y₁/y₂ = x₁/x₂, and recognize the graph as a straight line through the origin.

questions.stem: $y$ varies directly with $x$ (written $y \propto x$) means that there is a constant $m \neq 0$ such that …
solution: By definition: $y$ is said to vary directly with $x$, written $y \propto x$, when $y = mx$ where $m$ is a constant $\neq 0$.
$y = \frac{m}{x}$ (equivalently $xy = m$) is the inverse variation, and $y = x + m$ is neither.

questions.stem: The graphical representation of the direct variation $y = m x$ (where $m \neq 0$) is a straight line …
solution: Direct variation is a linear relation between $x$ and $y$: its graph is a straight line.
When $x = 0$, $y = m \times 0 = 0$, so the line passes through the origin point $(0, 0)$ — like the car's distance-time graph $d = 15t$.

questions.stem: If $y \propto x$ and $y = 12$ when $x = 4$, find the value of $y$ when $x = 7$.
solution: $y \propto x$ means $y = mx$ where $m$ is a constant $\neq 0$.
Substitute the given values: $12 = 4m$, so $m = 3$ and the relation is $y = 3x$.
When $x = 7$: $y = 3 \times 7 = 21$.

questions.stem: If $y \propto x$ and $y = 10$ when $x = 25$, find the value of $y$ when $x = 40$.
solution: $y = mx$; substitute: $10 = 25m$, so $m = \frac{10}{25} = \frac{2}{5}$.
The relation is $y = \frac{2}{5}x$.

questions.stem: If $y \propto x$ and $y = 18$ when $x = 27$, find the value of $x$ when $y = 8$.
solution: $y = mx$; substitute: $18 = 27m$, so $m = \frac{18}{27} = \frac{2}{3}$.
The relation is $y = \frac{2}{3}x$.
When $y = 8$: $8 = \frac{2}{3}x$, so $x = 8 \times \frac{3}{2} = 12$.

learning_objectives.label: Inverse variation
learning_objectives.description: Express y ∝ 1/x as xy = m, i.e. y = m/x (m constant ≠ 0), use y₁/y₂ = x₂/x₁, and recognize that the graph is not a straight line.

questions.stem: $y$ changes inversely with $x$ (written $y \propto \frac{1}{x}$) means that, for a constant $m \neq 0$, …
solution: By definition: $y$ changes inversely with $x$, written $y \propto \frac{1}{x}$, when $xy = m$ (m constant $\neq 0$), i.e. $y = \frac{m}{x}$.
$y = mx$ and $\frac{y}{x} = m$ both describe direct variation instead.

questions.stem: The graphical representation of the inverse variation $y = \frac{m}{x}$ is …
solution: The inverse relation is not a linear relation between the two variables $x$ and $y$.
So it is not represented by a straight line — plotting points such as $(3, 10), (5, 6), (6, 5), (10, 3)$ for $xy = 30$ shows a curve.
A line through the origin is the graph of DIRECT variation.

questions.stem: If $y \propto \frac{1}{x}$ and $y = 3$ when $x = 8$, find the value of $y$ when $x = 6$.
solution: $y \propto \frac{1}{x}$ means $y = \frac{m}{x}$ where $m$ is a constant $\neq 0$.
Substitute: $3 = \frac{m}{8}$, so $m = 24$ and the relation is $y = \frac{24}{x}$.

questions.stem: A rectangle has a constant area of $36$ cm². When its length is $4$ cm its width is $9$ cm. Find its width (in cm) when its length is $12$ cm.
solution: For a constant area, length × width = area, so width changes inversely with length: $xy = 36$.
When the length is $12$: $12 \times y = 36$.
$y = \frac{36}{12} = 3$ cm — tripling the length divided the width by 3.

questions.stem: If $y \propto \frac{1}{x}$ and $y = 5$ when $x = 4$, find the value of $x$ when $y = 2$.
solution: $y = \frac{m}{x}$; substitute: $5 = \frac{m}{4}$, so $m = 20$.
The relation is $y = \frac{20}{x}$, i.e. $xy = 20$.

learning_objectives.label: Identifying and applying variation
learning_objectives.description: Decide from a table or a rule whether two variables vary directly, inversely, or neither, and apply variation to real contexts (e.g. v = 9.8t in physics; a cylinder's height varying inversely with the square of its radius).

questions.stem: In the physics relation $v = 9.8\,t$ between velocity $v$ (m/sec) and time $t$ (sec), the kind of variation between $v$ and $t$ is …
solution: $v = 9.8\,t$ has the form $v = \text{constant} \times t$ with constant $9.8 \neq 0$.
So $v \propto t$: $v$ directly changes with $t$ (direct variation).

questions.stem: The table with $x: 2,\ 4,\ 8$ and $y: 6,\ 12,\ 24$ represents …
solution: Test $\frac{y}{x}$ for each pair: $\frac{6}{2} = 3$, $\frac{12}{4} = 3$, $\frac{24}{8} = 3$ — constant.
So $y = 3x$, which is the direct variation $y \propto x$.
($xy$ gives $12, 48, 192$ — not constant, so it is not inverse variation.)

questions.stem: The table with $x: 2,\ 4,\ 6$ and $y: 12,\ 6,\ 4$ represents …
solution: Test $xy$ for each pair: $2 \times 12 = 24$, $4 \times 6 = 24$, $6 \times 4 = 24$ — constant.
So $xy = 24$, i.e. $y = \frac{24}{x}$: this is the inverse variation $y \propto \frac{1}{x}$.
($\frac{y}{x}$ gives $6, 1.5, \frac{2}{3}$ — not constant, so it is not direct variation.)

questions.stem: The table with $x: 1,\ 2,\ 3$ and $y: 5,\ 7,\ 9$ represents …
solution: Test direct variation ($\frac{y}{x}$ constant): $\frac{5}{1} = 5$, $\frac{7}{2} = 3.5$, $\frac{9}{3} = 3$ — not constant.
Test inverse variation ($xy$ constant): $1 \times 5 = 5$, $2 \times 7 = 14$, $3 \times 9 = 27$ — not constant.
So the table represents neither direct nor inverse variation (in fact $y = 2x + 3$, a line that misses the origin).

questions.stem: The relation between velocity $v$ (m/sec) and time $t$ (sec) is $v = 9.8\,t$. Find the value of $t$ when $v = 49$ m/sec.
solution: $v = 9.8\,t$ is a direct variation with constant $9.8$.
Substitute $v = 49$: $49 = 9.8\,t$.
$t = \frac{49}{9.8} = 5$ seconds.

questions.stem: The height $h$ of a right cylinder of constant volume varies inversely as the square of its radius $r$. If $h = 32$ cm when $r = 3$ cm, find $h$ (in cm) when $r = 4$ cm.
solution: $h \propto \frac{1}{r^2}$ means $h = m \times \frac{1}{r^2}$ where $m$ is a constant $\neq 0$.
Substitute $h = 32$, $r = 3$: $32 = \frac{m}{9}$, so $m = 32 \times 9 = 288$.

learning_objectives.label: Resources of collecting data
learning_objectives.description: Distinguish primary (field) resources — interviews and questionnaires, accurate but costly in time/effort/money — from secondary (historical) resources — agencies (e.g. CAPMAS), internet, media — which save time and money.

questions.stem: A researcher collects data by distributing a questionnaire (survey) to families and interviewing them. This is a … resource of collecting data.
solution: Primary (field) resources are those from which we originally get the data ourselves, through interviewing or questionnaires (surveys).
A questionnaire distributed to families is exactly this case, so it is a primary (field) resource.
Secondary (historical) resources would be ready-made data from agencies, the internet or media.

questions.stem: A student takes ready-made data about Egypt's population from the records of the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics. This data comes from a … resource.
solution: Secondary (historical) resources are data we get from authorities and agencies that formally work in statistics, such as the central agency for mobilization and statistics, the internet and the media.
The student did not collect the data himself; he used the agency's ready records, so it is a secondary (historical) resource.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of secondary (historical) resources of collecting data?
solution: Secondary (historical) resources give us data that is already collected by agencies, the internet or the media.
Because the data is ready-made, this type of resource saves time and money.
Accuracy is the distinguishing advantage of primary (field) resources, and needing great time and effort is a disadvantage of primary resources — not of secondary ones.

questions.stem: Primary (field) resources of collecting data are distinguished by … but they …
solution: Primary (field) resources — interviewing and questionnaires — are distinguished by accuracy, because we collect the data originally ourselves.
However, they need time and effort, and conducting them is highly expensive.
So the correct completion is: distinguished by accuracy, but need much time, effort and money.

questions.stem: Four students collected data for a statistics project. Which student used a PRIMARY (field) resource?
solution: Primary (field) resources are those where we originally get the data ourselves through interviewing or questionnaires.
Only Mona collected data directly from the people concerned (interviewing shoppers), so she used a primary resource.
Newspapers, websites and agency tables are ready-made data — these are secondary (historical) resources.

learning_objectives.label: Methods of collecting data: mass population vs samples
learning_objectives.description: Compare the method of mass population (census: all the society, unbiased, very accurate, but long time/effort/cost) with methods of samples (save time/effort/money; the only way for gigantic societies and for destructive tests); recognize biased samples.

questions.stem: The method of collecting data that includes ALL the values of the statistical society is called the method of …
solution: The method of mass population means to collect the data related to the phenomenon from all the society (like a full population census).
It includes all the values, so it is unbiased and its outcomes are very accurate — but it needs long time, great effort and much money.

questions.stem: To collect data about the fish of the Mediterranean Sea, we must use the method of …, because the society is gigantic.
solution: One advantage of the methods of samples is that they are the only way to collect data about gigantic societies, like fish.
We cannot count or examine every fish in the sea, so we study a sample and generalize the outcomes on the whole society.

questions.stem: A factory checks the validity of the electric lamps it produces (how long a lamp can be used before getting burned) using a sample only. Why?
solution: The sample method is the only method to study some limited societies where the examination destroys the unit under test.
Knowing how long a lamp can be used means running it until it gets burned — so a tested lamp cannot be sold.
Testing all the production would destroy it; therefore the factory tests a sample only (like checking a patient's blood by a small sample).

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of the method of mass population?
solution: The method of mass population collects the data from all the society.
Because it includes all the values, it is unbiased and its outcomes are very accurate.
Saving time, effort and money — and studying gigantic societies — are advantages of the methods of samples, not of the mass population method.

questions.stem: A researcher selected a sample, but it does not represent all the society well, so the outcomes are not accurate. Such a sample is called …
solution: A disadvantage of the sample methods is that the outcomes are not accurate if the selected sample does not represent all the society well.
In such a case the sample is called biased.

learning_objectives.label: Biased vs random selection; simple random sample
learning_objectives.description: Distinguish biased (deliberate) selection from random selection where every member has an equal chance; apply the simple random sample to a homogeneous society (cards in a box for small societies; calculator random digits for big societies).

questions.stem: In random selection (random samples), the sample is selected such that …
solution: Random selection means to select a sample such that the chance of getting any value from the society is equal.
Selecting the sample deliberately to satisfy the research objectives is the biased selection, and including the whole society is the mass population method.

questions.stem: The simple random sample is the simplest type of samples, and it is taken from the … societies.
solution: The simple random sample is the simplest type of samples.
It is taken from the homogeneous societies, where selection is related only to the size and number of units in the society.
When the society is heterogeneous (made of different sets), we use the layer sample instead.

questions.stem: To choose 4 students from a class of 36, the teacher writes each student's name on an identical card, puts all the cards in a box, draws one card randomly, records it, returns it, and repeats until 4 different students are obtained. This sample is …
solution: All the cards are identical and are drawn randomly from the box, so every student has an equal chance of being selected.
This is exactly the simple random sample procedure for a small society: prepare identical cards, draw randomly, return the card, and repeat until the needed sample is obtained.
The class is one homogeneous group (no layers), so it is a simple random sample.

questions.stem: To know how the students understood a mathematics lesson, a teacher analyzed the test outcomes of ONLY the group of students who had studied that same topic together before. This selection is …
solution: The teacher selected the sample deliberately, in a way that satisfies the objectives of the research: only students who studied the same topic.
The other students had no chance of being selected, so the chances are not equal.
This is the biased selection (samples not randomly selected).

questions.stem: The students of a school are numbered from 1 to 600. To select a simple random sample, a calculator gave the random numbers $0.624,\ 0.871,\ 0.315,\ 0.598,\ 0.042$. After taking out the decimal point (making numbers from 0 to 999), how many of these five numbers can be used for the sample?
solution: Taking out the decimal point turns each number into a whole number from 0 to 999: $624,\ 871,\ 315,\ 598,\ 042 = 42$.
Only numbers within the field of the students' numbers (1 to 600) can be used; numbers more than 600 are taken out.
$624 > 600$ (rejected), $871 > 600$ (rejected), $315 \le 600$ (accepted), $598 \le 600$ (accepted), $42 \le 600$ (accepted).
So $3$ of the five numbers can be used.

learning_objectives.label: Layer (stratified) random sample
learning_objectives.description: For a heterogeneous society, divide it into homogeneous layers and select from each layer a random sample proportional to the layer's size in the society.

questions.stem: When the society to be examined is heterogeneous (made up of sets different in characteristics), we divide it into homogeneous sets and select from each one. The suitable sample is the … sample.
solution: When the society is heterogeneous, it is divided into homogeneous sets according to the characteristics forming it; each set is called a layer.
The researcher selects a random sample in which each layer is represented according to its size in the society — such a sample is called the layer sample.

questions.stem: A society consists of 600 persons where the ratio of males to females is $2 : 1$. To select a layer sample of 60 persons, how many males must be selected?
solution: The ratio of males to females is $2 : 1$, so the society consists of $2 + 1 = 3$ equal parts.
Each layer must be represented in the sample according to its size: the males' share is $\frac{2}{3}$ of the sample.
Number of males $= \frac{2}{3} \times 60 = 40$ persons (and the females are $\frac{1}{3} \times 60 = 20$).

questions.stem: A school has 900 students distributed over the three preparatory grades in the ratio $4 : 3 : 2$ (first : second : third). In a layer sample of 90 students, how many students of the THIRD grade must be selected?
solution: The society is heterogeneous (three different grades), so each grade is a layer represented according to its size.
The ratio parts total $4 + 3 + 2 = 9$ parts; the third grade's share is $\frac{2}{9}$.
Number of third-grade students in the sample $= \frac{2}{9} \times 90 = 20$ students.

questions.stem: A society of 1500 persons contains a layer of 600 persons. In a layer sample of 75 persons taken from the whole society, how many persons must come from that layer?
solution: In the layer sample, each layer is represented in the sample according to its size in the society.
The layer's share of the society $= \frac{600}{1500} = \frac{2}{5}$.
Number selected from that layer $= \frac{2}{5} \times 75 = 30$ persons.

questions.stem: In the layer random sample, each layer is represented in the sample according to …
solution: After dividing the heterogeneous society into homogeneous layers, the researcher selects a random sample from each layer.
Each layer is represented according to its size in the society — for example, a society of 400 with males : females $= 3 : 2$ and a sample of 50 gives 30 males and 20 females.
Equal shares regardless of size would not represent the society well (a biased sample).

learning_objectives.label: Dispersion and the range
learning_objectives.description: Explain dispersion (how divergent the values of a set are; zero dispersion means all values equal); compute the range = greatest value − smallest value; know its limits: influenced greatly by outliers and depends only on the two extreme values.

questions.stem: Find the range of the values: $7,\ 12,\ 9,\ 15,\ 10$.
solution: The range is the difference between the greatest value and the smallest value in the set.
The greatest value $= 15$ and the smallest value $= 7$.

questions.stem: If the dispersion of a set of values equals zero, then …
solution: Dispersion measures how divergent the values are — the differences between the values.
When the dispersion is zero, there are no differences between the values: all the values are equal.

questions.stem: The range of a set of values is 25 and its smallest value is 13. Find the greatest value.
solution: Range $=$ greatest value $-$ smallest value.
So greatest value $=$ range $+$ smallest value $= 25 + 13 = 38$.

questions.stem: The range does not give a clear picture of the dispersion of a set because it depends only on …
solution: The range is influenced only by the two extreme values: range $=$ greatest $-$ smallest.
It is not influenced by any value in the set except the greatest and smallest values, so it does not give a clear picture of the dispersion of the whole set.
It is also influenced greatly by the outlier.

questions.stem: For the set $41,\ 44,\ 46,\ 48,\ 90$: find how much the range DECREASES when the outlier 90 is removed from the set.
solution: Range of the whole set $= 90 - 41 = 49$.
After removing the outlier 90, the greatest value becomes 48, so the range $= 48 - 41 = 7$.
The decrease in the range $= 49 - 7 = 42$ — this shows that the range is influenced greatly by the outlier.

learning_objectives.label: Standard deviation of a set of values
learning_objectives.description: Compute σ = √(Σ(x−x̄)²/n): find the mean, the deviations from the mean, their squares, the average of the squares, then the positive square root.

questions.stem: The standard deviation $\sigma$ of a set of values is the positive square root of …
