solution: By definition, the standard deviation is the positive square root of the average of the squares of deviations of the values from the mean.
In symbols: $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n}}$, where $\bar{x}$ is the mean and $n$ is the number of values.

questions.stem: Find the standard deviation of the values: $6,\ 6,\ 6,\ 6$.
solution: The mean $\bar{x} = \dfrac{6+6+6+6}{4} = \dfrac{24}{4} = 6$.
Every deviation $x - \bar{x} = 6 - 6 = 0$, so $\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 = 0$.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{0}{4}} = 0$ — when all the values are equal, the dispersion is zero.

questions.stem: Calculate the standard deviation of the values: $7,\ 9,\ 10,\ 11,\ 13$.
solution: Find the mean: $\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum x}{n} = \dfrac{7+9+10+11+13}{5} = \dfrac{50}{5} = 10$.
Form the table of deviations $x - \bar{x}$: $-3,\ -1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 3$.
Square the deviations $(x - \bar{x})^2$: $9,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1,\ 9$, so $\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 = 20$.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{20}{5}} = \sqrt{4} = 2$.

questions.stem: The standard deviation of the values $3,\ 5,\ 5,\ 7$ equals …
solution: The mean $\bar{x} = \dfrac{3+5+5+7}{4} = \dfrac{20}{4} = 5$.
Deviations from the mean: $-2,\ 0,\ 0,\ 2$; their squares: $4,\ 0,\ 0,\ 4$, so $\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 = 8$.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{8}{4}} = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$.

questions.stem: For a set of 5 values, the sum of the squares of deviations from the mean is $\sum (x - \bar{x})^2 = 45$. Find the standard deviation.
solution: $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n}}$ where $n$ is the number of values.
Substitute: $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{45}{5}} = \sqrt{9}$.
$\sigma = 3$.

learning_objectives.label: Standard deviation of a frequency distribution
learning_objectives.description: Compute σ = √(Σ(x−x̄)²k / Σk) with x̄ = Σxk/Σk for a frequency distribution; for grouped data (sets/classes) use the center of each set as x.

questions.stem: When calculating the standard deviation of a frequency distribution of SETS (classes), $x$ in the formula $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x-\bar{x})^2\, k}{\sum k}}$ represents …
solution: In the frequency-distribution formula, $x$ represents the value or the center of the set, and $k$ represents the frequency of the value or the set.
For a distribution of sets (classes), we first find the center of each set and use it as $x$; $\sum k$ is the total of frequencies.

questions.stem: In the frequency distribution with sets $0-,\ 4-,\ 8-,\ 12-,\ 16\text{-}20$, find the center of the set $12-$.
solution: The center of a set is half the sum of its two boundaries: the set $12-$ extends from 12 to 16.

questions.stem: The following frequency distribution shows the goals scored in 10 football matches — goals: $0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4$; number of matches: $1,\ 1,\ 6,\ 1,\ 1$. Find the standard deviation of the number of goals.
solution: Total of frequencies $\sum k = 1+1+6+1+1 = 10$.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x-\bar{x})^2 k}{\sum k}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{10}{10}} = \sqrt{1} = 1$ goal.

questions.stem: The marks of 16 students are grouped in the sets $0-,\ 10-,\ 20\text{-}30$ with frequencies $2,\ 12,\ 2$. Find the standard deviation of the marks.
solution: Find the centers of the sets: $\dfrac{0+10}{2}=5$, $\dfrac{10+20}{2}=15$, $\dfrac{20+30}{2}=25$ — use them as $x$.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x-\bar{x})^2 k}{\sum k}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{400}{16}} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ marks.

questions.stem: The numbers of defective units found in 50 boxes: defective units $0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 4$ with numbers of boxes $5,\ 10,\ 20,\ 10,\ 5$. The standard deviation of the defective units equals …
solution: The mean $\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum xk}{\sum k} = \dfrac{100}{50} = 2$ units.
$\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{60}{50}} = \sqrt{1.2} \approx 1.095$ units — note $1.2$ alone (choice B) forgets the square root, and $2$ (choice A) is the mean, not $\sigma$.

learning_objectives.label: Comparing dispersion and homogeneity of data sets
learning_objectives.description: Use range and standard deviation to compare sets with the same measuring units and equal means: the set with the smaller standard deviation is more homogeneous (less dispersed); σ is affected by all values and carries the units of the data.

questions.stem: Two sets of data have the same measuring units and equal means. The MORE HOMOGENEOUS set is the one whose …
solution: The standard deviation is used to compare the dispersion of sets which have the same measuring units when the means are equal.
The set which has the greater standard deviation is more dispersed; so the more homogeneous set is the one with the smaller standard deviation.

questions.stem: In an exam, class A has mean 25 marks with $\sigma = 3.2$ marks, and class B has mean 25 marks with $\sigma = 5.6$ marks. Which statement is correct?
solution: The two distributions have the same units (marks) and equal means (25), so we compare their standard deviations.
$\sigma_A = 3.2 < \sigma_B = 5.6$, so class B's marks are more dispersed.
Therefore class A is more homogeneous in getting marks — equal means is exactly the condition that MAKES the comparison valid.

questions.stem: Set A: $10,\ 12,\ 14$ and Set B: $5,\ 12,\ 19$. How many times is the range of set B as great as the range of set A?
solution: Range of set A $= 14 - 10 = 4$.
Range of set B $= 19 - 5 = 14$.
$\dfrac{\text{range of B}}{\text{range of A}} = \dfrac{14}{4} = 3.5$ times — set B is more divergent (more dispersed) than set A.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the standard deviation is CORRECT?
solution: Notice (1): the standard deviation is affected by the deviations of ALL the values, and its value is affected by the outlier — unlike the range, which depends only on the two extremes.
Notice (2): the standard deviation has the same measuring units as the original data (e.g. marks, units, pounds).
So D is the correct statement.

questions.stem: Set A: $8,\ 9,\ 10,\ 11,\ 12$ and Set B: $6,\ 8,\ 10,\ 12,\ 14$ (both have mean 10). How many times is the standard deviation of set B as great as the standard deviation of set A?
solution: Both sets have mean $\bar{x} = \dfrac{50}{5} = 10$, so we compare dispersion by the standard deviation.
$\dfrac{\sigma_B}{\sigma_A} = \dfrac{2\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 2$ — set B is twice as dispersed, so set A is more homogeneous.

learning_objectives.label: Circular measure: degrees, minutes and seconds
learning_objectives.description: Use the degree as the circular measuring unit (1° = 60', 1' = 60''); convert between D° M' S'' form and decimal degrees, by hand and with the calculator.

questions.stem: One degree is divided into…
solution: The degree is the circular measuring unit, and its parts are: $1^\circ = 60'$ (minutes) and $1' = 60''$ (seconds).
So one degree is divided into 60 minutes.

questions.stem: Express $30'$ (thirty minutes) as a part of a degree, in decimal form.
solution: Since $1^\circ = 60'$, divide the minutes by 60 to convert to degrees.

questions.stem: Write $45^\circ\ 30'$ in degrees as a decimal number.
solution: Convert the minutes to degrees: $30' = \frac{30}{60} = 0.5^\circ$.
Add to the whole degrees: $45^\circ\ 30' = 45 + 0.5 = 45.5^\circ$.

questions.stem: $20.25^\circ$ written in degrees and minutes equals…
solution: The whole part stays as degrees: $20^\circ$.
Convert the decimal part to minutes: $0.25^\circ = 0.25 \times 60 = 15'$.
So $20.25^\circ = 20^\circ\ 15'$ — note $0.25^\circ$ is NOT $25'$, because a degree has 60 minutes, not 100.

questions.stem: Write $62^\circ\ 45'\ 36''$ in degrees as a decimal number.
solution: Convert the minutes: $45' = \frac{45}{60} = 0.75^\circ$.
Convert the seconds: $36'' = \frac{36}{3600} = 0.01^\circ$.

questions.stem: $28.51^\circ$ written in degrees, minutes and seconds equals…
solution: Convert the decimal part to minutes: $0.51^\circ = 0.51 \times 60 = 30.6'$.
Keep $30'$ and convert the remaining $0.6'$ to seconds: $0.6' = 0.6 \times 60 = 36''$.

learning_objectives.label: The main trigonometric ratios of an acute angle
learning_objectives.description: In a right-angled triangle, identify the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse for an acute angle; define sin = opposite/hypotenuse, cos = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan = opposite/adjacent.

questions.stem: In triangle $ABC$ right-angled at $B$: $\sin C =$ …
solution: For the acute angle $C$: the side opposite is $AB$, the side adjacent is $BC$, and the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle) is $AC$.
$\sin C = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{AB}{AC}$.
Careful: $\frac{BC}{AC}$ is $\cos C$ (adjacent over hypotenuse), not $\sin C$.

questions.stem: For an acute angle in a right-angled triangle, the tangent of the angle equals…
solution: The three main ratios are: $\sin = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$, $\cos = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$, $\tan = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$.
So the tangent is opposite ÷ adjacent — swapping them (adjacent ÷ opposite) is the classic mistake.

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $B$, with $AB = 3$ cm, $BC = 4$ cm and $AC = 5$ cm. Then $\cos C =$ …
solution: For angle $C$: adjacent side $= BC = 4$, hypotenuse $= AC = 5$.
$\cos C = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{4}{5}$.
($\frac{3}{5}$ is $\sin C$ and $\frac{3}{4}$ is $\tan C$ — don't mix opposite with adjacent.)

questions.stem: $XYZ$ is a triangle right-angled at $Y$, with $XY = 6$ cm, $YZ = 8$ cm and $XZ = 10$ cm. Then $\tan Z =$ …
solution: For angle $Z$: opposite side $= XY = 6$, adjacent side $= YZ = 8$.
$\tan Z = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{XY}{YZ} = \frac{6}{8} = \frac{3}{4}$.
($\frac{4}{3}$ comes from swapping opposite and adjacent — that would be $\tan X$, not $\tan Z$.)

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $B$. If $\sin C = 0.6$ and $AC = 15$ cm, find the length of $AB$ in cm.
solution: $\sin C = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{AB}{AC}$.
$AB = 0.6 \times 15 = 9$ cm.

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $B$, so $A$ and $C$ are two complementary acute angles. Then $\sin A =$ …
solution: For angle $A$: the opposite side is $BC$, so $\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC}$.
For angle $C$: the adjacent side is also $BC$, so $\cos C = \frac{BC}{AC}$.
The two ratios use the same sides, so $\sin A = \cos C$: the sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complementary angle.

learning_objectives.label: Computing trigonometric ratios in right triangles
learning_objectives.description: Use the Pythagorean theorem to find the missing side, then compute the ratios of the two acute angles; verify identities such as sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $C$, with $AC = 3$ cm and $BC = 4$ cm. Find the length of the hypotenuse $AB$ in cm.
solution: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, so it is $AB$.
By the Pythagorean theorem: $(AB)^2 = (AC)^2 + (BC)^2 = 9 + 16 = 25$.
$AB = 5$ cm.

questions.stem: For any acute angle $C$ in a right-angled triangle: $\sin^2 C + \cos^2 C =$ …
solution: Write the ratios with sides: $\sin C = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}}$ and $\cos C = \frac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}}$.
$\sin^2 C + \cos^2 C = \frac{\text{opp}^2 + \text{adj}^2}{\text{hyp}^2}$.
By the Pythagorean theorem $\text{opp}^2 + \text{adj}^2 = \text{hyp}^2$, so the ratio equals $1$.

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $C$, with $AB = 10$ cm and $BC = 8$ cm. Find $\sin B$ as a decimal.
solution: First find the missing side: $(AC)^2 = (AB)^2 - (BC)^2 = 100 - 64 = 36$, so $AC = 6$ cm.
For angle $B$: opposite side $= AC = 6$, hypotenuse $= AB = 10$.
$\sin B = \frac{AC}{AB} = \frac{6}{10} = 0.6$.

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $C$, with $AB = 25$ cm and $AC = 7$ cm. Then $\tan A =$ …
solution: Find the missing side: $(BC)^2 = (AB)^2 - (AC)^2 = 625 - 49 = 576$, so $BC = 24$ cm.
For angle $A$: opposite side $= BC = 24$, adjacent side $= AC = 7$.
$\tan A = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{24}{7}$. ($\frac{7}{24}$ is $\tan B$ — the opposite/adjacent swap.)

questions.stem: If $\theta$ is an acute angle and $\sin \theta = \frac{5}{13}$, then $\cos \theta =$ …
solution: Take a right triangle where the side opposite $\theta$ is 5 and the hypotenuse is 13.
The adjacent side $= \sqrt{13^2 - 5^2} = \sqrt{169 - 25} = \sqrt{144} = 12$.
$\cos \theta = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{12}{13}$.

questions.stem: If $\tan A = \frac{3}{4}$ where $A$ is an acute angle, find the value of $25 \sin A \cos A$.
solution: $\tan A = \frac{3}{4}$ means opposite $= 3$ and adjacent $= 4$ in a right triangle; the hypotenuse $= \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$.
So $\sin A = \frac{3}{5}$ and $\cos A = \frac{4}{5}$.
$25 \sin A \cos A = 25 \times \frac{3}{5} \times \frac{4}{5} = 25 \times \frac{12}{25} = 12$.

learning_objectives.label: Exact trigonometric ratios of 30°, 45° and 60°
learning_objectives.description: Derive the exact ratios from the half-equilateral triangle (sides 1 : 2 : √3) and the isosceles right triangle (sides 1 : 1 : √2); recall the table of exact values.

questions.stem: $\sin 30^\circ =$ …
solution: In the half-equilateral triangle the sides are in ratio $1 : 2 : \sqrt{3}$, and the side opposite $30^\circ$ is the shortest one.
$\sin 30^\circ = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{1}{2}$.
($\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is $\sin 60^\circ$ — don't swap the two.)

questions.stem: $\tan 45^\circ =$ …
solution: In the isosceles right triangle the two legs are equal ($1 : 1 : \sqrt{2}$).
$\tan 45^\circ = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}} = \frac{1}{1} = 1$.

questions.stem: $\cos 60^\circ =$ …
solution: In the half-equilateral triangle, the side adjacent to the $60^\circ$ angle is the shortest side (ratio 1) and the hypotenuse is 2.
$\cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}$. ($\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is $\cos 30^\circ$.)

questions.stem: $\tan 30^\circ =$ …
solution: In the half-equilateral triangle: side opposite $30^\circ$ is 1, side adjacent to $30^\circ$ is $\sqrt{3}$.
$\tan 30^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$. ($\sqrt{3}$ is $\tan 60^\circ$ — the reciprocal.)

questions.stem: Find the value of: $2 \sin 30^\circ + \tan 45^\circ$.
solution: Substitute the exact values: $\sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}$ and $\tan 45^\circ = 1$.

questions.stem: $ABC$ is a triangle right-angled at $B$, with $m(\angle C) = 30^\circ$ and $AC = 8$ cm. Find the length of $AB$ in cm.
solution: $AB$ is the side opposite angle $C$, and $AC$ is the hypotenuse.
$\sin C = \frac{AB}{AC}$, so $\sin 30^\circ = \frac{AB}{8}$.
$AB = 8 \times \frac{1}{2} = 4$ cm.

learning_objectives.label: Evaluating expressions with special angles
learning_objectives.description: Evaluate numeric expressions in sin, cos and tan of 30°, 45°, 60°; use sin θ = cos (90° − θ) and tan θ = sin θ / cos θ.

questions.stem: $\sin 30^\circ = \cos \dots^\circ$
solution: The sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complementary angle (the two angles add up to $90^\circ$).
$30^\circ + 60^\circ = 90^\circ$, so $\sin 30^\circ = \cos 60^\circ$ (both equal $\frac{1}{2}$).

questions.stem: For any acute angle $A$: $\tan A =$ …
solution: $\frac{\sin A}{\cos A} = \frac{\text{opp}/\text{hyp}}{\text{adj}/\text{hyp}} = \frac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}} = \tan A$.
Check with $A = 30^\circ$: $\frac{1/2}{\sqrt{3}/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \tan 30^\circ$ ✓.

questions.stem: Find the value of: $\sin 60^\circ \cos 30^\circ - \sin 30^\circ$ (as a decimal).
solution: Substitute the exact values: $\sin 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\cos 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, $\sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}$.
As a decimal: $0.25$.

questions.stem: Find the value of: $\tan^2 60^\circ + \tan^2 45^\circ$.
solution: $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}$, so $\tan^2 60^\circ = 3$.
$\tan 45^\circ = 1$, so $\tan^2 45^\circ = 1$.

questions.stem: Find the value of: $\left(\cos^2 45^\circ + \sin^2 30^\circ\right) \div \tan^2 30^\circ$ (as a decimal).
solution: $\cos 45^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, so $\cos^2 45^\circ = \frac{1}{2}$; and $\sin^2 30^\circ = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4}$.
The bracket $= \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{4}$.
$\tan 30^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, so $\tan^2 30^\circ = \frac{1}{3}$; dividing: $\frac{3}{4} \div \frac{1}{3} = \frac{3}{4} \times 3 = \frac{9}{4} = 2.25$.

questions.stem: The value of $\dfrac{\sin 60^\circ \tan 60^\circ - \sin 30^\circ}{\cos^2 30^\circ}$ is…
solution: Numerator: $\sin 60^\circ \tan 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \sqrt{3} = \frac{3}{2}$, then $\frac{3}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = 1$.
Denominator: $\cos^2 30^\circ = \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{3}{4}$.

learning_objectives.label: Finding the acute angle given its trigonometric ratio
learning_objectives.description: Recover the angle from an exact special-angle ratio or with the calculator inverse keys, expressing answers in degrees, minutes and seconds.

questions.stem: If $\sin X = \frac{1}{2}$ where $X$ is an acute angle, then $m(\angle X) =$ …
solution: From the special-angle table, the acute angle whose sine is $\frac{1}{2}$ is $30^\circ$.
So $m(\angle X) = 30^\circ$. (It is $\cos 60^\circ$ that equals $\frac{1}{2}$, not $\sin 60^\circ$.)

questions.stem: If $\tan X = 1$ where $X$ is an acute angle, then $m(\angle X) =$ …
solution: $\tan 45^\circ = 1$ (the two legs of the isosceles right triangle are equal).
So $m(\angle X) = 45^\circ$.

questions.stem: If $\cos X = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ where $X$ is an acute angle, find $m(\angle X)$ in degrees.
solution: From the special-angle table, $\cos 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
So $m(\angle X) = 30^\circ$.

questions.stem: If $\tan (X + 15^\circ) = \sqrt{3}$ where $X$ is an acute angle, find $m(\angle X)$ in degrees.
solution: $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}$, so $X + 15^\circ = 60^\circ$.
$X = 60^\circ - 15^\circ = 45^\circ$, which is an acute angle ✓.

questions.stem: If $\tan 3X = \sqrt{3}$ where $3X$ is an acute angle, find $m(\angle X)$ in degrees.
solution: $\tan 60^\circ = \sqrt{3}$, and $3X$ is acute, so $3X = 60^\circ$.
$X = \frac{60^\circ}{3} = 20^\circ$.

learning_objectives.label: Trigonometry in geometric applications
learning_objectives.description: Apply trigonometric ratios inside geometric figures (isosceles and equilateral triangles): drop a perpendicular, then find angles, sides and areas.

questions.stem: $ABC$ is an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC = 10$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. $\overline{AD} \perp \overline{BC}$ where $D \in \overline{BC}$. Then $\cos B =$ …
solution: In an isosceles triangle, the perpendicular from the vertex bisects the base, so $D$ is the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$ and $BD = 6$ cm.
Triangle $ABD$ is right-angled at $D$: for angle $B$, adjacent $= BD = 6$ and hypotenuse $= AB = 10$.
$\cos B = \frac{BD}{AB} = \frac{6}{10} = \frac{3}{5}$. ($\frac{4}{5}$ would be $\sin B$.)

questions.stem: $ABC$ is an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC = 10$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. $\overline{AD} \perp \overline{BC}$ where $D \in \overline{BC}$. Find $\sin B$ as a decimal.
solution: $D$ is the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$, so $BD = 6$ cm.
In right triangle $ABD$: $(AD)^2 = (AB)^2 - (BD)^2 = 100 - 36 = 64$, so $AD = 8$ cm.
$\sin B = \frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{8}{10} = 0.8$.

questions.stem: $ABC$ is an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC = 10$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. Find the area of the triangle in cm².
solution: Draw $\overline{AD} \perp \overline{BC}$; then $D$ is the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$ and $BD = 6$ cm.
Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times BC \times AD = \frac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 8 = 48$ cm².

questions.stem: $ABC$ is an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC = 10$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. $\overline{AD} \perp \overline{BC}$ where $D \in \overline{BC}$. Find $\tan (\angle CAD)$ as a decimal.
solution: $D$ is the midpoint of $\overline{BC}$, so $CD = 6$ cm, and $AD = \sqrt{100 - 36} = 8$ cm.
In right triangle $ACD$ (right-angled at $D$): for angle $CAD$, opposite $= CD = 6$ and adjacent $= AD = 8$.
$\tan (\angle CAD) = \frac{CD}{AD} = \frac{6}{8} = 0.75$.

questions.stem: The height of an equilateral triangle whose side length is $6$ cm equals…
solution: The height from a vertex makes a right triangle in which the side of the triangle is the hypotenuse and the base angle is $60^\circ$.
Height $= 6 \sin 60^\circ = 6 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 3\sqrt{3}$ cm.

learning_objectives.label: The distance between two points
learning_objectives.description: Find the distance between two points using the distance rule: on the x-axis |x2−x1|, on the y-axis |y2−y1|, and in general MN = √((x2−x1)²+(y2−y1)²) via the Pythagorean theorem; distance of M(x1,y1) from the origin O = √(x1²+y1²).

questions.stem: The two points $A(2, 0)$ and $B(6, 0)$ are both located on the x-axis. The length of $\overline{AB} =$ … unit length.
solution: The two points are both located on the x-axis, so the distance is the absolute difference of the x-coordinates: $AB = |x_2 - x_1|$.
So $AB = 4$ unit length.

questions.stem: Find the length of $\overline{CD}$ where $C(0, -2)$ and $D(0, 3)$.
solution: The two points are both located on the y-axis (both have $x = 0$), so $CD = |y_2 - y_1|$.
So $CD = 5$ unit length.

questions.stem: Find the distance between the two points $M(1, 2)$ and $N(4, 6)$.
solution: The distance between two points $(x_1, y_1)$, $(x_2, y_2) = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$.
$MN = 5$ unit length.

questions.stem: The distance of the point $M(6, 8)$ from the origin point $O(0, 0)$ equals … unit length.
solution: The distance of a point $M(x_1, y_1)$ from the origin $O(0, 0)$ is $OM = \sqrt{x_1^2 + y_1^2}$ (Remark, Lesson 5-1).
$OM = 10$ unit length — note that $100$ forgets the square root and $14$ just adds the coordinates.

questions.stem: If the distance between the two points $A(3, y)$ and $B(6, 4)$ is $5$ unit length, and $y > 0$, find the value of $y$.
solution: Apply the distance rule: $AB = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$, so $\sqrt{(6-3)^2 + (4-y)^2} = 5$.
Square both sides: $9 + (4 - y)^2 = 25$, so $(4 - y)^2 = 16$.
Then $4 - y = 4$ or $4 - y = -4$, giving $y = 0$ or $y = 8$.
Since $y > 0$, we take $y = 8$.

learning_objectives.label: Applying the distance rule to geometric figures
learning_objectives.description: Use the distance rule to prove properties of figures: identify squares/rhombi/rectangles by side and diagonal lengths, right triangles by the converse of the Pythagorean theorem, points on a circle equidistant from its center, and collinear points where AB + BC = AC.

questions.stem: The triangle whose vertices are $A(1, 1)$, $B(4, 1)$ and $C(4, 5)$ is right-angled at …
solution: By the converse of the Pythagorean theorem, the angle opposite to $\overline{AC}$ is right, so the triangle is right-angled at $B$.

questions.stem: Find the surface area of the triangle whose vertices are $A(1, 1)$, $B(4, 1)$ and $C(4, 5)$, in square units.
solution: From the distance rule: $AB = \sqrt{(4-1)^2 + (1-1)^2} = 3$ and $BC = \sqrt{(4-4)^2 + (5-1)^2} = 4$.
$(AB)^2 + (BC)^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = (AC)^2$, so the triangle is right-angled at $B$ (converse of the Pythagorean theorem).
Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times AB \times BC = \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 4 = 6$ square units.

questions.stem: A circle has center $O(0, 0)$ and passes through the point $(3, 4)$. Which of the following points does NOT lie on this circle?
solution: The radius is the distance from the center to $(3, 4)$: $r = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$.
A point lies on the circle when its distance from the center equals $5$: $(5,0) \to \sqrt{25} = 5$ ✓; $(0,-5) \to \sqrt{25} = 5$ ✓; $(-4,3) \to \sqrt{16+9} = 5$ ✓.
$(4, 4) \to \sqrt{4^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{32} \neq 5$, so $(4, 4)$ does not lie on the circle.

questions.stem: If the four points $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ have all four sides equal in length AND the two diagonals equal in length, then the figure $ABCD$ is a …
solution: Equal sides make the figure a rhombus (Drill, Lesson 5-1).
If in addition the two diagonals are equal in length, the rhombus is a square.
This is exactly the check used in Example 1: sides all $\sqrt{41}$ and diagonals both $\sqrt{82}$ prove a square.

questions.stem: For the points $A(0, 0)$, $B(3, 4)$ and $C(6, 8)$: $AB = 5$, $BC = 5$ and $AC = 10$. Since $AB + BC = AC$, the three points are …
solution: Check the distances with the rule: $AB = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$, $BC = \sqrt{(6-3)^2 + (8-4)^2} = 5$, $AC = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$.
When the sum of two distances equals the third, the middle point lies on the segment joining the other two: the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are collinear — they cannot form a triangle at all.

learning_objectives.label: Coordinates of the midpoint of a segment
learning_objectives.description: Find the two coordinates of the midpoint of a line segment with ends (x1,y1), (x2,y2): M((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2), including segments parallel to the axes.

questions.stem: The coordinates of point $C$, the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ where $A(2, 6)$ and $B(4, 0)$, are …
solution: The midpoint of the segment with ends $(x_1, y_1)$, $(x_2, y_2)$ is $M\left(\dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$.
$C\left(\dfrac{2 + 4}{2}, \dfrac{6 + 0}{2}\right) = C\left(\dfrac{6}{2}, \dfrac{6}{2}\right)$.

questions.stem: Find the x-coordinate of the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ where $A(-3, 5)$ and $B(7, 1)$.
solution: The x-coordinate of the midpoint is $x = \dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}$.
(The full midpoint is $(2, 3)$, since $y = \dfrac{5 + 1}{2} = 3$.)

questions.stem: The segment with the two ends $A(-4, -1)$ and $B(-4, -7)$ is parallel to the y-axis. The coordinates of its midpoint are …
solution: Both ends have $x = -4$, so the segment is parallel to the y-axis and its midpoint keeps $x = -4$.
So the midpoint is $(-4, -4)$.

questions.stem: The origin point $O(0, 0)$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ where $A(a, 3)$ and $B(5, b)$. Find the value of $a + b$.
solution: Apply the midpoint rule to each coordinate: $\dfrac{a + 5}{2} = 0$ and $\dfrac{3 + b}{2} = 0$.
From the first: $a + 5 = 0$, so $a = -5$.
From the second: $3 + b = 0$, so $b = -3$.
Therefore $a + b = -5 + (-3) = -8$.

questions.stem: If $M(3, k)$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ where $A(1, 2)$ and $B(5, 6)$, find the value of $k$.
solution: The midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ is $\left(\dfrac{1 + 5}{2}, \dfrac{2 + 6}{2}\right) = (3, 4)$.
Comparing with $M(3, k)$: $k = 4$.

learning_objectives.label: Using the midpoint rule
learning_objectives.description: Use the midpoint rule in reverse to find an unknown endpoint given the midpoint, and apply it to parallelograms: the diagonals bisect each other, so their intersection point is the midpoint of both diagonals.

questions.stem: If $C(2, 1)$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ where $A(-1, 3)$, then the coordinates of point $B$ are …
solution: Consider $B(x_2, y_2)$. Since $C$ is the midpoint: $x = \dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}$ and $y = \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2}$.
Therefore $B(5, -1)$.

questions.stem: $C(0, 2)$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$ where $A(4, -2)$. Find the y-coordinate of point $B$.
solution: Consider $B(x_2, y_2)$; the midpoint rule gives $y = \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2}$.

questions.stem: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram where $A(1, 2)$, $B(4, 3)$ and $C(5, 6)$. The coordinates of point $D$ are …
solution: In a parallelogram the two diagonals bisect each other, so the intersection point $M$ is the midpoint of both $\overline{AC}$ and $\overline{BD}$.
$M$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AC}$: $M\left(\dfrac{1+5}{2}, \dfrac{2+6}{2}\right) = M(3, 4)$.
$M$ is also the midpoint of $\overline{BD}$ with $D(x_1, y_1)$: $3 = \dfrac{4 + x_1}{2}$ gives $x_1 = 2$, and $4 = \dfrac{3 + y_1}{2}$ gives $y_1 = 5$.
Therefore $D(2, 5)$.

questions.stem: In the parallelogram $ABCD$, the point at which the two diagonals intersect is …
solution: In a parallelogram, the two diagonals bisect each other.
So their intersection point $M$ is the midpoint of the diagonal $\overline{AC}$ and at the same time the midpoint of the diagonal $\overline{BD}$ — this is the property used to find a missing vertex.

questions.stem: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram where $A(2, -1)$ and $C(6, 3)$. If $M$ is the point of intersection of its two diagonals, find the sum of the two coordinates of $M$.
solution: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so $M$ is the midpoint of $\overline{AC}$.
Sum of the coordinates $= 4 + 1 = 5$.

learning_objectives.label: The slope of a straight line
learning_objectives.description: Compute the slope through two points m = (y2−y1)/(x2−x1); slope = tan E where E is the positive angle the line makes with the positive direction of the x-axis; sign of the slope by angle type (acute → m>0, obtuse → m<0, zero → m=0, right → undefined).

questions.stem: Find the slope of the straight line passing through the two points $(1, 2)$ and $(3, 6)$.
solution: The slope of the straight line passing through $(x_1, y_1)$, $(x_2, y_2)$ equals $\dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$.

questions.stem: If a straight line makes an ACUTE positive angle with the positive direction of the x-axis, then its slope is …
solution: From the table of Lesson 5-3: when the positive angle the line makes with the positive direction of the x-axis is acute, the slope is larger than zero.
(Obtuse angle → slope smaller than zero; zero angle → slope equal to zero; right angle → slope unidentified.)

questions.stem: The slope of the straight line passing through the two points $(2, -1)$ and $(2, 3)$ is …
solution: $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \dfrac{3 - (-1)}{2 - 2} = \dfrac{4}{0}$, and division by zero is undefined.
The two points have the same x-coordinate, so the line is vertical: it makes a right angle with the positive direction of the x-axis, and its slope is unidentified.

questions.stem: Find the slope of the straight line that makes a positive angle of measure $45°$ with the positive direction of the x-axis.
solution: The slope of a straight line $= \tan E$, where $E$ is the positive angle the line makes with the positive direction of the x-axis.

questions.stem: If the slope of the straight line passing through the two points $(3, k)$ and $(5, 7)$ equals $2$, find the value of $k$.
solution: Apply the slope rule: $m = \dfrac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \dfrac{7 - k}{5 - 3} = \dfrac{7 - k}{2}$.

learning_objectives.label: Slopes of parallel straight lines
learning_objectives.description: If L1 ∥ L2 then m1 = m2 and vice versa; lines parallel to the x-axis have slope 0, lines parallel to the y-axis have equal x-coordinates (undefined slope).

questions.stem: If $L_1 \parallel L_2$ and their slopes are $m_1$, $m_2$, then …
solution: If two lines are parallel, then their slopes are equal, and vice versa (Lesson 5-3).
So $L_1 \parallel L_2 \Rightarrow m_1 = m_2$ — the two lines make equal positive angles with the positive direction of the x-axis, and $\tan E_1 = \tan E_2$.

questions.stem: The straight line passing through the two points $(2, -1)$ and $(6, 3)$ is parallel to the straight line that makes with the positive direction of the x-axis an angle of measure …
solution: The slope of the line through the two points: $m_1 = \dfrac{3 - (-1)}{6 - 2} = \dfrac{4}{4} = 1$.
The slope of the line making angle $E$: $m_2 = \tan E$. Two lines are parallel when $m_1 = m_2$.
$\tan 45° = 1 = m_1$, so the line is parallel to the line making a $45°$ angle.

questions.stem: If the straight line $\overleftrightarrow{AB} \parallel$ the y-axis, where $A(x, 4)$ and $B(2, 9)$, find the value of $x$.
solution: A straight line parallel to the y-axis is vertical: all its points have the same x-coordinate.

questions.stem: If the straight line $\overleftrightarrow{CD} \parallel$ the x-axis, where $C(1, -3)$ and $D(6, y)$, find the value of $y$.
solution: A straight line parallel to the x-axis is horizontal: all its points have the same y-coordinate (its slope is $0$).

questions.stem: The straight line passing through $(0, 0)$ and $(2, 4)$ is parallel to the straight line passing through $(1, 1)$ and $(a, 5)$. Find the value of $a$.
solution: Slope of the first line: $m_1 = \dfrac{4 - 0}{2 - 0} = 2$.
The lines are parallel, so $m_2 = m_1 = 2$: $\dfrac{5 - 1}{a - 1} = 2$.

learning_objectives.label: Slopes of perpendicular straight lines
learning_objectives.description: If L1 ⊥ L2 then m1 × m2 = −1 and vice versa; use the product rule to find perpendicular slopes and to prove a triangle is right-angled at a vertex.

questions.stem: If $L_1 \perp L_2$ and their slopes are $m_1, m_2 \in \mathbb{R}^*$, then $m_1 \times m_2 =$ …
solution: The product of multiplying the slopes of two perpendicular straight lines $= -1$, and vice versa (Lesson 5-3).
So $L_1 \perp L_2 \Rightarrow m_1 \times m_2 = -1$.

questions.stem: The slope of the straight line perpendicular to the straight line passing through the two points $(1, 1)$ and $(3, 5)$ equals …
solution: Slope of the given line: $m_1 = \dfrac{5 - 1}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2$.
For the perpendicular line: $m_1 \times m_2 = -1$, so $2 \times m_2 = -1$.

questions.stem: A straight line of slope $m$ is perpendicular to a straight line of slope $-4$. Find the value of $m$ (as a decimal).
solution: For perpendicular lines: $m_1 \times m_2 = -1$.

questions.stem: The triangle $XYZ$ has vertices $X(1, 4)$, $Y(2, 1)$ and $Z(5, k)$, and it is right-angled at $Y$. Find the value of $k$.
solution: Slope of $\overleftrightarrow{XY}$: $m_1 = \dfrac{1 - 4}{2 - 1} = -3$.
Slope of $\overleftrightarrow{YZ}$: $m_2 = \dfrac{k - 1}{5 - 2} = \dfrac{k - 1}{3}$.
The triangle is right-angled at $Y$, so $\overleftrightarrow{XY} \perp \overleftrightarrow{YZ}$ and $m_1 \times m_2 = -1$: $-3 \times \dfrac{k - 1}{3} = -1$.

questions.stem: The straight line passing through the two points $(0, 3)$ and $(3, 0)$ is perpendicular to the straight line that makes with the positive direction of the x-axis an angle of measure …
solution: Slope of the first line: $m_1 = \dfrac{0 - 3}{3 - 0} = -1$.
Slope of the line making angle $E$: $m_2 = \tan E$; for $E = 45°$, $m_2 = \tan 45° = 1$.
$m_1 \times m_2 = -1 \times 1 = -1$, so the two straight lines are perpendicular.

learning_objectives.label: The equation y = mx + b: slope and y-intercept
learning_objectives.description: Read the slope m (coefficient of x) and the y-intercept b from y = mx + b; convert ax + by + c = 0 (b ≠ 0) to that form, where m = −a/b = −(coefficient of x)/(coefficient of y).

questions.stem: In the equation of the straight line $y = mx + b$, the symbol $b$ denotes …
solution: The equation of the straight line with respect to its slope $(m)$ and the y-intercept $(b)$ is $y = mx + b$ (Definition, Lesson 5-4).
$m$ is the slope (the coefficient of $x$) and $b$ is the length of the y-intercept — the part between the origin and the point where the line cuts the y-axis.

questions.stem: Find the slope of the straight line whose equation is $y = 3x - 2$.
solution: The equation is in the formula $y = mx + b$, where $m$ is the slope.
The coefficient of $x$ is $3$, so the slope $= 3$ (and the y-intercept $= -2$).

questions.stem: Find the length of the y-intercept of the straight line whose equation is $2x + y - 6 = 0$.
solution: Write the equation in the formula $y = mx + b$: from $2x + y - 6 = 0$ we get $y = -2x + 6$.
The y-intercept is the constant term: $b = 6$.
(Check: at $x = 0$, $y = 6$, so the line cuts the y-axis at $(0, 6)$.)

questions.stem: The slope of the straight line whose equation is $2x + 5y - 10 = 0$ equals …
solution: For the equation in the formula $ax + by + c = 0$, $b \neq 0$: the slope $m = \dfrac{-a}{b} = \dfrac{-\text{coefficient of } x}{\text{coefficient of } y}$.
(Or rearrange: $5y = -2x + 10$, so $y = -\dfrac{2}{5}x + 2$ — same slope, y-intercept $2$.)

questions.stem: For the straight line whose equation is $4x - 2y + 6 = 0$: if $m$ is its slope and $b$ is the length of its y-intercept, find the value of $m + b$.
solution: Slope: $m = \dfrac{-a}{b} = \dfrac{-4}{-2} = 2$.
Rearrange to $y = mx + b$: $2y = 4x + 6$, so $y = 2x + 3$, giving the y-intercept $b = 3$.

learning_objectives.label: Finding the equation of a straight line
learning_objectives.description: Write the equation of a line given its slope and a point on it (substitute to find c in y = mx + c), including lines parallel or perpendicular to a given line and lines bisecting a given segment (through its midpoint).

questions.stem: The equation of the straight line whose slope is $2$ and whose y-intercept is $5$ is …
solution: Substitute directly in the formula $y = mx + b$ with $m = 2$ and $b = 5$.
The equation is $y = 2x + 5$.

questions.stem: A straight line of slope $3$ passes through the point $(1, 2)$. If its equation is $y = 3x + c$, find the value of $c$.
solution: The line passes through the point $(1, 2)$, so the point satisfies the equation.
Substitute: $2 = 3 \times 1 + c$.
$c = 2 - 3 = -1$, so the equation is $y = 3x - 1$.

questions.stem: The equation of the straight line passing through the point $(0, 4)$ and parallel to the straight line $y = 2x - 1$ is …
solution: Parallel lines have equal slopes, so the required slope $m = 2$.
The line cuts the y-axis at $(0, 4)$, so its y-intercept $b = 4$.
Substitute in $y = mx + b$: the equation is $y = 2x + 4$.

questions.stem: The equation of the straight line passing through the point $(2, 1)$ and perpendicular to the straight line passing through the two points $(1, 5)$ and $(3, 1)$ is …
solution: Slope of the line through $(1, 5)$ and $(3, 1)$: $m_1 = \dfrac{1 - 5}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{-4}{2} = -2$.
The required line is perpendicular to it, so $m_1 \times m_2 = -1$: $-2 \times m_2 = -1$, giving $m_2 = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
Write $y = \dfrac{1}{2}x + c$; the line passes through $(2, 1)$, so $1 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 + c = 1 + c$, giving $c = 0$.
The equation is $y = \dfrac{1}{2}x$.

questions.stem: If $A(0, 1)$, $B(2, 5)$ and $C(4, 3)$, then the equation of the straight line passing through the vertex $A$ and bisecting $\overline{BC}$ is …
solution: The line bisects $\overline{BC}$, so it passes through its midpoint: $\left(\dfrac{2 + 4}{2}, \dfrac{5 + 3}{2}\right) = (3, 4)$.
Slope of the required line through $A(0, 1)$ and $(3, 4)$: $m = \dfrac{4 - 1}{3 - 0} = 1$.
Write $y = mx + c$: the line passes through $A(0, 1)$, so $c = 1$.
The equation is $y = x + 1$.
